info.title: Thread-safe external UI updates for Pathland signals

parts.text:
I got the follwing suggestion. Tell me what you think. Feature: safe, ergonomic external UI updates (actor-thread signal handoff)
Context
Pathland 0.2.1, as used by Quarkus 3.39+ and Spring Boot hosts. Views are authored in the Kotlin DSL with WritableSignal, computed, and effect. Pathland signals are documented as single-threaded by contract, and PathlandRegistry serializes all session work on a single actor thread.
Problem
External event sources — Kafka/SmallRye @Incoming consumers, scheduled jobs, DB notifications, websocket clients, etc. — run on non-Pathland threads. There is no supported way to update a live session’s signal from such a thread.
A signal injected into the Pathland environment can physically be set from a consumer thread, but that runs the emitter/binding effects and delta generation on the consumer thread while the session actor may be rendering the same tree. That is a data race. The current public alternatives are all unsatisfactory:
- an explicit UI Refresh button (requires a user click),
- resync(...), which only re-emits the retained tree and does not re-run body(),
- reflection into private registry/session state,
- client-side script hacks.
This is a common server-driven-UI requirement and should be a first-class Pathland feature.
Goal
Add a thread-safe, non-blocking API for external code to update live Pathland UIs while preserving the actor model and producing normal fine-grained deltas.
Proposed design
1. Core actor primitive
Add an explicit actor handoff to the server core:
public interface PathlandSession {
    /** Safe from any thread; runs on this session's actor. */
    void submit(Runnable task);
}

public final class PathlandRegistry {
    Set<String> sessionIds();
    void submitAll(Consumer<PathlandSession> action);
    AutoCloseable onSession(Consumer<PathlandSession> onOpen,
                            Consumer<PathlandSession> onClose);
}
Requirements: work is serialized on the existing actor, dropped after shutdown, and exceptions are logged without killing the session.
2. App-level signal hub
Provide an app-scoped hub with a canonical value and per-session mirrors:
public interface PathlandSignalHub {
    /** Safe from any thread; non-blocking, coalescing. */
    <T> void publish(String name, T value);

    <T> WritableSignal<T> appSignal(String name, T initial);
}
- publish never touches a session’s reactive graph directly.
- It schedules, per subscribed session, an update of that session’s local WritableSignal on the session actor.
- The local signal triggers the existing effect/delta path.
- Latest-wins per (session, signal); bounded queues; metrics for published/coalesced/dropped.
- Subscribe on session open, unsubscribe on close; no work after close.
3. Environment integration
Bind a session-scoped SessionSignals object at the root, similar to Platform.ACTIVE_PATH:
EnvironmentKey<SessionSignals> SESSION_SIGNALS =
        EnvironmentKey.of("pathland.sessionSignals");

public interface SessionSignals {
    <T> Signal<T> signal(String name, T initial);
    void submit(Runnable task);
}
View usage:
val count = Environment.value(SESSION_SIGNALS)
    .signal("customer-events.count", 0)

Text(computed { "Customer events consumed: ${count.get()}" })
External producer:
@Incoming("customer-channel")
void onCustomer(CustomerCreatedEvent event) {
    hub.publish("customer-events.count", counter.incrementAndGet());
}
The host should bind SessionSignals automatically; app authors should not need per-session plumbing.
4. Multi-node
Design publish to be node-agnostic. A follow-up can back it with Redis pub/sub or a versioned state store, with each node fanning out to its local sessions. Ignore stale/duplicate updates. Pathland already has pathland-state-redis to build on.
Non-goals / constraints
- Do not make WritableSignal.set asynchronous or magically thread-safe; keep its synchronous semantics.
- Do not share one global WritableSignal across sessions without per-effect actor dispatch; that creates cross-session races.
- No breaking changes to existing public APIs; prefer additive APIs.
- Keep both Quarkus and Spring Boot hosts working; the core must stay framework-agnostic.
- No unbounded queues or blocking producers.
Acceptance criteria
- A Kafka/SmallRye consumer can call hub.publish("counter", n) from its worker thread, and a live view’s computed text updates via a small delta — no Refresh button, no resync.
- All signal reads, writes, and effect execution occur on the session actor thread; add an assertion/test for this.
- Multiple sessions receive independent updates; closing a session cancels pending updates.
- Rapid updates coalesce to the latest value without unbounded memory growth.
- Works in both Quarkus and Spring Boot test harnesses; include a Quarkus test with a background thread and a multi-session test.
- Docs: API documentation plus a short “external updates” guide using the Kafka example; update any relevant spec/architecture notes.
Relevant files
- lib/java/pathland-server-core/src/main/java/dev/pathland/server/PathlandRegistry.java
- lib/java/pathland-server-core/src/main/java/dev/pathland/server/PathlandSession.java
- lib/java/pathland-server-core/src/main/java/dev/pathland/server/PathlandHost.java
- lib/java/pathland-view-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/pathland/view/core/signal/ (Signal, WritableSignal, Signals, Effect, Scheduler)
- lib/java/pathland-view-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/pathland/view/core/Environment.kt
- lib/java/pathland-view-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/pathland/view/core/EnvironmentBinding.kt
- lib/java/pathland-quarkus/src/main/java/dev/pathland/quarkus/PathlandRegistryProducer.java
- lib/java/pathland-spring-boot-starter/
- Existing tests under lib/java/pathland-server-core/src/test/ and lib/java/pathland-quarkus/src/test/
Suggested implementation order
1. Add submit / onSession / sessionIds to the server core with tests.
2. Add PathlandSignalHub, session-local mirrors, and automatic environment binding; add unit and integration tests.
3. Add coalescing metrics and shutdown/close behavior.
4. Add the Kafka example and docs.
5. Discuss Redis-backed fan-out as a follow-up.
First step
Read the current registry/session/emitter/signal/environment implementation, then propose a concrete implementation plan — API names, files, tests, and any spec conflicts — before writing code.

parts.text:
Now I understand the architecture. Let me check the documentation about signals single-threaded and whether there's a notion of "registry actor". Also the StateStores/InMemory. And how the emitters handle SSR on request threads concurrently with the actor - the Scheduler is `@Synchronized` global, ReactiveContext thread-local. But an emitter's effect execution for a live session happens on actor. SSR creates a throwaway emitter on request thread; its signals are distinct. Only shared Scheduler is synchronized. So the proposal to run external updates on actor is correct.

Now let me assess the proposal deeply.

Key observations / critique:

1. The core `submit(Runnable)` on PathlandSession is right, but the proposal's `submit` semantics need care: if called from the actor thread itself (e.g., within an effector event), submitting would enqueue rather than run inline. Also exceptions logged not kill session. Also need to guard against `PathlandRegistry.execute`'s private nature. Should be straightforward.

2. `Set<String> sessionIds()` and `submitAll(Consumer<PathlandSession>)` — exposing session ids is problematic: sessions are lazily created and keyed by per-connection uiId; exposing ids leaks internal identity and creates a coupling. More importantly, `sessionIds()` snapshot can race; a session could close right after. Better: `onSession` listener (register open/close callbacks) and per-session handle. Or `forEachSession(Consumer)` that runs each action on its own actor. `submitAll` runs "on each session's actor" — needs to be defined; it should just schedule per session. But there's a subtlety: the registry has a single actor thread for all sessions, so submitAll enqueuing N tasks on the same actor could starve inbound events (a hot producer + many sessions). That's a real concern. Currently all sessions share one actor thread per registry. A "publish" that schedules per subscribed session update could flood the single actor. Coalescing helps, but need a per-session bounded pending map and only schedule one task per session per tick.

3. The app-level `PathlandSignalHub` design: canonical value + per-session mirrors. This is sound and the right shape (avoid sharing one WritableSignal across sessions). But the API `appSignal(String name, T initial)` is confusing: what is a canonical app signal? It says canonical value and per-session mirrors. Need clarity on how the initial value is established and how a new session gets the current canonical value rather than a stale initial. Also what about session-local writes / read-modify-write? The hub's `publish` only supports set semantics. Fine.

4. Environment integration `SessionSignals` with `signal(name, initial)`: this has a subtle issue — the `initial` passed at view render is per render; if the hub has a canonical value, the view's initial should only be the fallback for a signal not yet published. But if a component re-renders after the value changed, `signal()` is invoked again with the original initial; it must return the existing per-session signal (keyed by name), not reset. Need session-scoped signal registry keyed by name. Also, typed generic name collisions: two views using same name with different types will ClassCastException; should document name as app-global and type-stable, or make the key include type. 

5. Environment `signal` returning `Signal<T>` vs `WritableSignal<T>`: Proposal says `Signal<T>`. But app code may need to write locally. The text shows `val count = Environment.value(...).signal(...)` and then `count.get()`. Fine. But if external publish is the only writer, read-only is good (enforces discipline). However session-local effects/state may need writes; keep a separate `SessionSignals.submit` for arbitrary runnables.

6. Critical: `Environment.value(SESSION_SIGNALS)` is a `Signal<SessionSignals>`; is `SessionSignals` bound as a scoped environment value? Need `EnvironmentBinding.with(e -> e.key(SESSION_SIGNALS).value(sessionSignals))` at mount in PathlandSession, like ACTIVE_PATH. That changes PathlandSession constructor. But `Environment` object is created per mount; EnvironmentValues thread-local. Since the root is mounted once with a binding, all views under it get it. Good. But note `Environment.value` without an environment binding returns `EnvironmentSignal` that captures at first get; if used outside the bound subtree (e.g., in a computed after?) it may work, but need care.

7. Automatic host binding: the registry needs to create/attach the hub to sessions. But `PathlandHub` is app-scoped. `PathlandApp` is the natural place? The proposal says "host should bind SessionSignals automatically". How does the hub find sessions? Registry subscribes on session open/close. But the hub is app-scoped while registry is per-mount; there may be multiple registries (Mounts) and the same app. Need a `PathlandSignalHub` bean produced by the starters, wired into registry. Also SSR sessions: a hub publish during SSR? SSR is a throwaway session, not registered. `SessionSignals` should work on SSR too (return initial/canonical) but not subscribe. Need to decide.

8. The proposal says `publish` "never touches a session's reactive graph directly" and "schedules, per subscribed session, an update". But if a session has no live connection (SSR or pending before first message) it's not subscribed, so its first render won't have the published value unless the hub's canonical value is read at `signal(name, initial)` creation. This requires the hub to have the canonical map, and `SessionSignals.signal(name, initial)` should seed from hub's canonical value when first created. Otherwise a new session shows `initial` not latest. The design mentions "canonical value" but doesn't spell out seeding. Must be explicit.

Also what about subscription timing: session subscribes on open but sessions are created lazily on first message, and the root view is mounted at session construction. If the hub subscribes after mount, a publish between construction and subscription is missed, but seeding at signal creation handles it. Good.

9. Coalescing/bounded queues: "Latest-wins per (session, signal); bounded queues" — if it's a per-name map of latest values, that's naturally bounded by number of distinct names, not by publishes. That's good. But the current design has a single actor per registry; a `publish` loops over all sessions, updating a per-session `ConcurrentHashMap<String, Object>` and schedules one task per session. With thousands of sessions and a high-frequency producer, you'll enqueue up to N tasks per publish (coalesced within a tick only if you check "already scheduled"). Need a per-session `AtomicBoolean`/dirty flag to ensure at most one pending flush task per session. Also, the actor queue is unbounded (singleThreadExecutor), so a storm of publishes from external threads could still enqueue unboundedly across sessions. But with per-session pending-set + scheduled flag, at most one task per session is queued at a time. Good. Also consider backpressure metrics.

But there's a more subtle issue: the actor is shared across all sessions in a registry. A single external producer publishing to many sessions will enqueue N flush tasks; each flush sets potentially multiple signals and emits. That's inherent. Consider batching all sessions in one actor task (a single flush task that drains a global pending map) to reduce overhead. `submitAll` could post one task that iterates all dirty sessions. But per-session error isolation and connect/send cost... Could be okay.

10. "All signal reads, writes, and effect execution occur on the session actor thread" — Good acceptance test. But note the emitter's `Scheduler` is global and also used by SSR request threads. The test should assert per-session effect execution thread, not global. Also `Scheduler.flush` is `@Synchronized` and runs the effect on the calling thread; if an SSR write happens, it flushes on the request thread, but affects only throwaway subtree. Fine.

11. Non-goals are good. Additive.

12. Multi-node: hub publish is node-agnostic; Redis fan-out follow-up. Fine, but note state store already exists, and `PersistentState` is per-window; the hub is different (ephemeral). Good to keep separate.

13. Naming: `PathlandSignalHub` + `SessionSignals` — maybe `PathlandEventHub` or `PathlandUpdateHub` because it's not just signals; it's external update handoff. But signal hub is OK. `sessionIds()` is dangerous. `onSession` AutoCloseable subscription is good and safer than ids. `submitAll` possibly replace with `hub.publish` doing fan-out. But there is a use case for arbitrary code per session via `onSession` + `session.submit`.

14. Spec conflicts: This is a Java/server-core feature, not protocol. Should not touch spec/opcode. But AGENTS.md says status.md must be updated. Also, `AGENTS.md` says signals single-threaded; adding `submit` preserves it. No spec conflict, but document in status.md. There may be a need to note thread-safety contract in `Signal` KDoc.

15. Deployment: Quarkus/Spring wiring: need `PathlandSignalHub` bean. The proposal mentions `PathlandRegistryProducer`. Also, Spring Boot starter path is `lib/java/pathland-spring-boot-starter/src/main/java/com/pathland/spring/` — let me check actual path.

Let me check the Spring starter structure and whether there's an existing "Managed registry". Also check the version 0.2.1 mention — pom version.

Also check if there's a `PathlandApp` listener concept. Let me check StateStores and PersistentState quickly for thread-safety and "state signals" writes. Also check `View` and `Component` state to see if external writes possible. But enough.

Let me verify Spring starter path and look at its config.

No web-framework dependency — framework glue lives in the starters. ## Implemented - **Security hardening (issue #63)**: `WindowIds` validates the client-supplied `wid` (≤128 chars, `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`; a colon is rejected so it cannot collide with the mount-qualified state scope). Invalid ids are treated as absent (SSR defaults) or replaced with a fresh UUID on the WebSocket. `InboundRateLimiter` bounds inbound batches/bytes per connection before actor work is queued (`pathland.max-inbound-batches-per-second`, default 500; `pathland.max-inbound-bytes-per-second`, default 2 MiB) and reports drops via `PathlandTelemetry.inboundDropped` (`pathland.inbound.dropped`). The SSR script tag now carries `integrity="sha384-…"` from the manifest's second line (`PathlandAssets.bundleIntegrity()`); an older one-line manifest simply omits it. - **Attributed text transport**: `FrameRebase` rebases `SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT`'s string-section offset (like `SET_TEXT`) for delta batching/frame merging, and `ProxyIdMap` remaps its node id. - **Window metadata + SSR head attrs**: `PathlandSession.renderHtml` injects host attrs into the renderer's opening `` (which now carries `lang`), and `FrameRebase` rebases `SET_WINDOW_METADATA` string offsets. Proxy origin metadata is dropped with the other META opcodes. - **Per-route SEO metadata (issue #45)**: `PageMetadata`/`PageMetadataRequest` carry canonical URL, Open Graph/Twitter cards, and JSON-LD. `PathlandApp` gains a default `pageMetadata(request)` hook (active mount-stripped route + host canonical URL); `PathlandRegistry.renderHtml(route, wid, hostDefaults)` merges host defaults with the app's per-route overrides before SSR. Let me check the StateStores/redis and whether there's an app-scoped "context". Also check the `PathlandApp` interface. And check whether the version 0.2.1 is the current; yes. Let me look at the `InMemoryStateStore`/`RedisStateStore` perhaps to see if there's a pub/sub or a versioned pattern. But likely enough.

Let me also examine whether the registry does any session lookup by id that could be exposed safely. And check for tests of lifecycle hooks.

Main task: give opinion. Given plan mode, I should produce a well-formed plan. But the user said "Tell me what you think." So answer with assessment + concrete plan guidance. I should be concise but thorough enough. The system says keep responses short (<4 lines) unless detail requested. Here the user asks for thoughts on a proposal; detail is warranted. But plan mode requests a plan. I'll produce an evaluation with concrete corrections, then a proposed implementation plan, and ask a couple of clarifying questions.

Let me verify a few technical concerns:

- `Scheduler` is global static, `@Synchronized`. If external thread writes a signal directly, effect may run on external thread. Correct diagnosis.
- `PathlandRegistry` actor thread: `execute` private. `submit` needed.
- The environment binding: `EnvironmentValues` thread-local, set during render. So a view reading `Environment.value(SESSION_SIGNALS)` gets it; binding in root. Good.

Potential issue with `SessionSignals.signal(name, initial)`: If called during a `computed { }` body or effect, `signal()` creation is a side effect but that's fine (registry lookup). But it must be idempotent. Also must not be called from multiple threads; only on actor. If app code calls it on actor during body, fine.

Key design issue: where does the hub's canonical value live and how does a session-local signal get seeded? Also, what about a session that publishes from *within* the actor (e.g., a button handler that wants to update app-wide signal)? That should update canonical hub value and fan out to all sessions, including self. But self-update while on actor is synchronous; must avoid re-entrancy and double flush. Should support `publish` from actor thread too (not deadlock). Since `publish` is non-blocking and just updates canonical + schedules, on the actor thread it can apply locally immediately or schedule; Scheduler flush is reentrant-safe? `Scheduler.schedule` is `@Synchronized`, flush guards `flushing`. If publish called during an effect flush from app code (allowSignalWrites effect), scheduling another effect is fine (queued, flush at end). But the hub's per-session update should ideally be immediate on actor. Simplicity: publish always updates canonical map (ConcurrentHashMap) and enqueues per-session flush; on the actor thread, the queue is the same executor, so it'll be a subsequent task. That's fine but adds latency. Could detect actor thread and apply inline. But note `submit` should never block; inline-on-actor is fine.

Bigger concern: The hub's `publish` fanning out to *all* sessions of *all* registries. App-scoped hub is created by starter, but mounted apps share a registry per mount; a hub per app would need to know its registries. `PathlandApp` is the app; `PathlandHost` maps MountedApp → registry. A global hub bean is simplest for single-app hosts; but multi-app hosts need per-app hubs or a hub that's wired to a specific app. The proposal's `SessionSignals` is bound by `PathlandSession`, which is created by a registry for a specific app, so the app-scoped hub is resolvable via `PathlandApp` if `PathlandApp` gains a `signalHub()` hook. But that's an API change (additive default method) and changes `PathlandApp`. Alternatively, hub is a singleton bean and all sessions subscribe to it, with signal names namespaced by app. In multi-mount, the same hub would fan out to all sessions of all apps; wrong if two apps use the same name. Need an app or mount scope. I should flag this as the most important design hole.

Options:
A. Registry-owned hub (per mount). `PathlandRegistry` creates a `DefaultSignalHub`; expose `registry.signalHub()`. App gets it via... it doesn't have registry at body() time. But `SessionSignals` in environment gives the per-session view; external producers need the hub. Starter could expose `PathlandHub` (one bean) and forward publish to all registries; that's app-agnostic fan-out. For single-app this is fine. For multi-app, namespacing or per-mount hub beans.
B. Hub attached to `PathlandApp` (default method `signalHub()`) so each app owns its hub; registry reads `app.hub()` and sessions subscribe. This is clean and app-scoped, and the same hub bean can be injected into the app object or is created by the app. Add default `PathlandApp.signalHub()` returning a lazily created default. But `PathlandApp` is a SAM-like interface `View newRoot()` — adding a default method is additive. However, app instances are user-created (lambdas); a default method with lazy init requires a concrete default class. Possible.
C. Starter produces `PathlandSignalHub` and passes it to `PathlandHost`/registry constructors. Then all registries share it. For multi-app, the hub is app-agnostic, so name collisions across apps: document that names are global, or add a mount prefix internally. Actually the cleanest: hub is app-scoped by making registry register sessions with a hub scoped to that registry's app; the starter creates one hub per registry? But then external code needs access. Could produce a `PathlandHubs` registry keyed by mount.

I think the important thing for the review is to flag that "app-scoped hub" needs a concrete ownership model given multi-app hosting (`PathlandHost`). I'll propose registry-owned hub with a host-level router, or `PathlandApp`-owned.

Another issue: `submit(Runnable)` on `PathlandSession` exposes arbitrary code execution on the session actor. But `PathlandSession` objects are only obtainable via callbacks; fine. However the proposed `onSession(Consumer<PathlandSession>, Consumer<PathlandSession>)` from registry: `onOpen` is invoked on the actor thread when session created. If it calls `session.submit(...)`, that enqueues. Fine. But if `onClose` is invoked on actor during `close`, and it calls `submit`, it'll be dropped after shutdown. Fine.

`sessionIds()`: recommend not exposing; use `onSession` + `forEachSession`. Also `activeSessions()` exists.

`submitAll(Consumer<PathlandSession>)`: recommend `forEachSession` that schedules per-session; or hub fan-out. Also note if invoked from external thread, each consumer runs on the respective actor. But since one actor per registry, `submitAll` called on registry enqueues N tasks. Fine but bounded.

`PathlandSession.submit` should also handle the case where session is closed: a `closed` flag checked on actor. Currently `PathlandSession.close()` sets connection null etc. but no closed flag. Need `closed` boolean to drop tasks after close (the proposal says "dropped after shutdown"). Add.

`PathlandSession` doesn't know if it's on actor. `submit` should capture the registry's actor? PathlandSession is created by registry, but also created directly in tests and SSR. If `submit` is on the session, it needs an executor reference. For SSR throwaway sessions, cancellation. Best: pass a `SessionScheduler`/`Executor` from registry into session constructor; default direct-execution executor for standalone sessions (tests) so `submit` runs inline. Or keep `submit` default to run inline unless wired. But inline from external thread on a standalone session isn't actor semantics; but standalone session has no actor anyway. For safety, default to a single-thread executor or reject? Given the session is used in tests/SSR, a default `Runnable::run` is pragmatic but then external callers of a standalone session aren't protected. Document that `submit` is thread-safe only when the session is registry-owned; or always require a scheduler passed in. Better: `PathlandSession` gets an `Executor` (or `Actor`) constructor param, registry passes its actor; direct default for standalone. Then `submit` = executor.execute with closed + exception handling. But the registry's `execute` also has shutdown guard. Need to route through registry, not just raw executor. So maybe `PathlandSession.submit` delegates to a `TaskScheduler` interface provided by registry (with `execute(Runnable)`), default inline. This avoids exposing registry.

Also exception handling: `submit` tasks should be wrapped in try/catch logging, not propagate. But note the actor's `runOnActor` currently doesn't catch exceptions from tasks — `execute` tasks can throw and kill the single thread? `ExecutorService.execute` with a throwing task: the worker thread's uncaught handler ... in `ThreadPoolExecutor`, a task that throws terminates the worker; the pool creates a new worker for subsequent tasks (for `execute`). So not catastrophic but log needed. The proposal's submit wrapper catches and logs. Good.

Effects: `EffectException` from signal flush. Catch it. Since `Emitter` registers effects and `Scheduler.flush` throws, a signal write on the actor could throw; wrapping logs. But partial emission might have happened. Acceptable, but better to let the session survive.

Now "acceptance criteria: all signal reads, writes, and effect execution on session actor thread; add an assertion/test for this." Emitter mount happens in `PathlandSession` constructor on actor (for live) and on request thread for SSR. For live session, yes. External hub update runs on actor. Good.

Coalescing: "Rapid updates coalesce to the latest value" — with hub canonical map + per-session pending map. Must ensure the update applies the latest *at flush time*, not at publish time: store latest in the pending map, and the flush reads the pending map. If publish A then B before flush, flush applies B. If publish A, flush applies A, publish B, flush B → both, which is correct (latest-wins per tick, no loss of distinct values). Fine.

Metrics: add telemetry methods: `signalPublished(mount, name, subscribers)`, `signalUpdateCoalesced`, `signalUpdateDropped(reason)`. Or a generic `externalUpdate(...)`. Keep additive default methods. Note `PathlandTelemetry` is framework-agnostic, and `MicrometerTelemetry` needs updating + status.md.

Multi-node: don't build in v1; make `publish` an interface so it can be backed by a cluster later. But note if using a `DefaultSignalHub`, the hub's canonical state is in one JVM. Cluster fan-out can wrap it.

Documentation: add `docs`? Check where docs live. Let me check.

I have enough. Now let me think about the review and construct the plan.

Actually, let me double-check one thing: the proposal says "Environment.value(SESSION_SIGNALS)". The environment key type is `EnvironmentKey<SessionSignals>`. Fine. But `Environment.value` is a `Signal<T>` computed per lookup; binding a `SessionSignals` object (not a signal) works via `toSignal`.

Potential issue: The session signals must be accessible in `body()` for every component; the binding is at root, so yes.

But one thing: `Environment` scoping is thread-local via `Environment.within` during render. If a computed body runs later, it uses the environment captured at the component's slot (`slot.envScope`). So the binding is retained. Good.

Another design flaw: `SessionSignals.signal(name, initial)` called inside a `body()`/`computed` must be safe to call repeatedly (during re-renders). It returns the same session-local signal. But creating a signal during a computed body and reading it is fine. However, if a session-level signal is created lazily on first read during a computed, then a hub publish before first read won't have a local signal to update; but the pending map can be keyed by name and applied when the signal is created (seed from hub canonical). Or simpler: session always seeds new local signals from the hub canonical value; and pending updates are applied to existing local signals. Race: publish arrives after signal creation but before subscribe? If subscription is set up at session construction (before mount), then all good. The session can subscribe to the hub before mount (in constructor) so subsequent publishes are queued; mount's signal creation seeds from canonical anyway.

But note: mounting happens in `PathlandSession` constructor; the session isn't in the registry's `sessions` map until after construction (registry.session() does `new PathlandSession(...)` then `sessions.put`). If the hub subscribes per registry `sessionOpened`, that's after construction. Better to pass the hub into the session and subscribe in the constructor before mount. So `PathlandSession` needs the hub (or a `SessionSignalSource`) constructor param. That's an additive overload with a default no-op hub. Good.

SSR: throwaway session created in `renderHtml`; subscribing it to the hub would add overhead and be closed immediately; but for correctness of first paint, read canonical values at signal creation. No subscription needed. But if a publish happens during SSR, no update needed for a one-shot render? Actually SSR renders once; if publish happens after the initial read, the HTML may be stale on first paint, then the live session corrects it via WS. That's acceptable. But seeding canonical at signal creation is important.

Now `publish` fan-out requires knowing sessions. A hub attached to registry via constructor; registry calls `hub.register(sessionSignals)` on session construction and `hub.unregister` on close (on actor). Hub keeps a `ConcurrentHashMap<SessionSignals, ...>` or a set of mirrors. Then `hub.publish(name, value)` updates canonical and iterates mirrors scheduling the actor task. Each mirror needs the scheduler (`session.submit`). So `SessionSignals`/mirror holds a `submit` function. That's clean.

Alternative: registry-owned hub list accessible by host. But external producer needs the hub bean. Simplest: the starter creates a `DefaultPathlandSignalHub` singleton and passes it to `PathlandHost`/each registry. Multi-app: one singleton hub, sessions from all apps subscribe; signal names are app-global. Document. Or namespace by mount internally when registering (`registry.mountPath() + ":" + name`) so `hub.publish` from an app that has one mount works. But an external producer doesn't necessarily know which mount. Hmm. Could have `PathlandHost.signalHub(mountPath)` or app-scoped factory. Let me propose `PathlandApp.hub()` default or `PathlandHost` exposes `hubs()`. 

I think the best clean approach: **registry owns a hub**, and `PathlandHost` exposes access:
- `PathlandRegistry.signalHub()` → `PathlandSignalHub` for that app/mount.
- `PathlandHost.signalHub(String mountPath)` / `hubs()`.
But a single-app starter user wants `@Inject PathlandSignalHub hub;`. The starter can produce a `PathlandSignalHub` bean that is the hub for the root mount (or fail if multiple mounts without qualification). Multi-app can use `@Named`/qualifier or the host. Or better: **the hub is created by the application** (`PathlandApp` implements `signalHub()` via default) so it's naturally app-scoped and can be a CDI/Spring bean the app injects. Then registry uses `app.signalHub()`. The default implementation creates a `DefaultSignalHub`. But a default method creating a new hub per call is bad; need a stable field. Could add a separate `PathlandHub` bean and default lookup from a global static — ugly.

Maybe the cleanest: keep the hub in server-core as a standalone object constructed by the app and provided through `MountedApp`/`PathlandApp`? Let me look at how `PathlandApp` is supplied: it's a bean; apps are usually lambdas `() -> new MyHomeView()`. To let external code publish, the app must expose the hub bean. So the hub should be a separate bean, and `PathlandApp` should optionally expose it. Add a default method `default PathlandSignalHub signalHub() { return null; }`. The starter/registry: if `app.signalHub() != null`, sessions register. If the user wants external updates, they implement it:

```java
@Bean PathlandApp app(PathlandSignalHub hub) { return new MyApp(); }
```
That's awkward because the lambda cannot capture... actually it can: `return () -> new MyHomeView(hub)` and apps need hub access. Better a separate `PathlandApp` class with a hub field.

Simplest ergonomic: **the starter produces a singleton `PathlandSignalHub` and injects it into every registry** (hub is global to the process). Sessions register with it on construction. For multi-app, signal names are namespaced by mount inside the hub registration so `publish` targets all apps? No — if hub is global, `publish("x", v)` updates every session of every app. That may actually be desired? No. But multi-app is a secondary concern; document that the hub is process-wide and names should be unique across apps (or provide `publishFor(mount, name, value)`). I'd recommend the hub expose `publish` and a mount-scoped variant later. I'll raise it as a decision for the user: process-wide hub vs per-app.

Given the review asks mainly "what do you think", I'll frame the ownership question as the main design decision to settle.

Now let me think about whether `PathlandSession.submit` should be public at all or whether `SessionSignals.submit` + hub suffice. The proposal includes both. Public `submit(Runnable)` is useful for external code that has a session handle (via onSession). But it exposes the actor. It's a low-level primitive and acceptance criteria reference it. Keep it.

`sessionIds()` + id lookup risk: no way to get session by id currently publicly. If you add `sessionIds()` but no `session(id)`, it's useless. `onSession` is enough. Recommend dropping `sessionIds()` and `submitAll`; instead `onSession` returns an `AutoCloseable` and the callback is invoked for current sessions immediately plus future ones. `onSession` should invoke `onOpen` for existing sessions (on their actor) so late subscribers get current sessions. This mirrors event bus semantics and avoids `sessionIds`.

Also note the `onSession` callback should be resilient to slow consumers; tasks run on actor, fine.

Testing plan:
- server-core unit: `PathlandSessionSubmitTest` (submit from many threads → serialized; closed drops; exception logged/session survives).
- `SignalHubTest`: publish from N threads, per-session mirrors, latest-wins coalescing, close cancels.
- Actor-thread assertion: a `ThreadRecorder` captures `Thread.currentThread()` inside a view `computed`/effect and inside `SessionSignals.signal` reads after publish.
- Quarkus integration test with a background thread; Spring test similar.
- Multi-session isolation.

Now docs/status: update `lib/java/pathland-server-core/status.md`, `pathland-view-core/status.md` maybe, starters status, AGENTS.md? The AGENTS.md is an AI guide; maybe add a bullet. Also docs/ guide. The proposal says update relevant spec/architecture notes; but this is not protocol. Note no `spec/` change.

Let me now formulate the response. The user is likely the maintainer. I should be direct and critical: "The diagnosis is right; the design is 80% right; here are the holes." Then enumerate.

Let me be careful about one important technical fact: because the registry has **one actor thread for all sessions**, the hub fan-out via per-session `submit` doesn't actually give per-session parallelism; everything is serialized. That's fine, but means `publish` to N sessions adds N tasks to one queue. Coalescing per session is essential. Also a slow effect in session A delays updates for session B. That's already true for input dispatch. But external producers could starve the actor. Recommend a single coalesced "flush dirty sessions" task rather than N tasks, or at least a bounded per-session pending + one scheduled task per session. And a rate limit/backpressure: if the actor queue grows (can't easily inspect), use a max pending count and drop with a metric. Since `publish` is called from external threads and the actor queue is unbounded, a burst could OOM the task queue. Coalescing per session caps tasks at one per session *while pending*. But if publish happens after each flush completes, you get one task per publish per session — that's inherent and bounded by producer rate only if flushes keep up. To bound, the hub can use an `ArrayBlockingQueue`-free design: a per-session `AtomicBoolean scheduled`; publish sets latest value and, if not scheduled, schedules; the flush loops: drain latest until no newer value, then unschedule. This caps queued tasks at 1 per session. Memory bounded by names × sessions (latest value). Good. But if the producer publishes faster than flushes, each flush still processes the latest, so no unbounded task growth. Good — this addresses "no unbounded queues."

But `publish` also needs to work for sessions that don't yet have a mirror (SSR). Fine.

What about "canonical app signal": `appSignal(name, initial)` returns a `WritableSignal` for app code. But if we have a canonical hub map, who owns the canonical value and initial? The first `appSignal`/`publish` sets it; later conflicting initial ignored. Fine. But exposing a canonical `WritableSignal` that external threads must not set directly is confusing. Maybe drop `appSignal` in v1; just `publish` + per-session `signal` + session `submit`. Keep scope minimal. I'd recommend not shipping `appSignal` until there's a clear use case; it invites the exact cross-thread write the feature is meant to prevent. If kept, make it `Signal<T>` (read-only) or document only settable on the actor.

Also naming/type safety: `signal(name, initial)` with generics erased; if two views use the same name with different initial types, ClassCastException at read. Suggest a typed key or document; or key by `(name, type)` and validate first-use class equals subsequent. A `SignalKey<T>` object (like `EnvironmentKey`) would be safer: `SessionSignals.signal(SignalKey<Long> key, long initial)` where `SignalKey.of("customer-events.count")`. But external publish then needs the same key: `hub.publish(KEY, value)`. This gives compile-time types and avoids collisions, at the cost of a shared constant. This is a nice improvement: reuse `EnvironmentKey`-like pattern. The proposal's string name is convenient for cross-language normalizations, but a typed key is safer. I'd suggest `SignalKey<T>` (or allow string for convenience with runtime type check). Note the external producer and the view must share the key object/constant; that's normal.

Also, publish should be typed: `<T> void publish(SignalKey<T> key, T value)`, not string+G. If using strings, `<T> void publish(String name, T value)` erases and mismatch possible.

Another point: "The local signal triggers the existing effect/delta path." Yes, but the emitter's node bindings use effects registered in `Scheduler`; the flush is synchronous. The delta batcher coalesces for ~20ms. Good.

Also, "Latest-wins per (session, signal); bounded queues; metrics for published/coalesced/dropped." Good.

Now the `onSession` API: an `AutoCloseable onSession(...)` is good but should it also give `onClose`? The proposal's signature is fine. But `onOpen` runs on the actor; if the callback registers a collector, it must not block. Fine.

One more concern: `PathlandSession.submit` when called from the actor thread (e.g., within `onSession` onOpen) and the task mutates signals: if `submit` enqueues, it's deferred; acceptable. But `onOpen` might want to seed a signal immediately (before mount?) Actually onOpen is after construction/mount, so the session is already mounted. Publishing immediately after open schedules an update; fine.

What about shutdown ordering: `PathlandRegistry.shutdown` closes sessions on actor then shuts down the executor. `submit` after `shuttingDown` must drop. The hub should unregister all sessions on close. If a publish races `close`, the scheduled task checks the session's closed flag and drops. Good.

Now perhaps the most fundamental point: **Is this better solved at the environment/hub layer than at the session layer?** Yes; but the actor primitive is necessary. The design is good.

One more: `PathlandRegistry` has one actor for all sessions; SSR renders on request threads. The proposal says "all signal reads, writes, effect execution on the session actor." For SSR (throwaway), it's on the request thread, which is fine because it's isolated. The acceptance test should exclude SSR. Note this explicitly.

Potential conflict with `AGENTS.md` "renderers must not retain app state": no conflict, the hub is app-side.

Spec conflict: none; but `spec/ENGINE.md` says signals single-threaded? Let me check if spec mentions threading. Let me grep.

The user said "Tell me what you think." I'll give my opinion, then the plan. Since it's plan mode, I should ask clarifying questions at the end rather than implement.

Let me be precise about file paths.

Key critique points, ranked:
1. Session ownership / hub scope in multi-app hosts is unresolved. `PathlandHost` supports multiple mounted apps, each with own registry; a single global hub would cross-publish. Need explicit ownership: hub owned by `PathlandApp` (default method) or registry, exposed via host. 
2. Seeding new sessions from canonical value, and subscription timing (subscribe before mount; SSR seeds canonical). Otherwise new sessions show stale `initial`.
3. `sessionIds()` + `submitAll()` are unsafe/leaky. Use `onSession` with current-session replay; drop `sessionIds`. `submitAll` should be `forEachSession` and coalesce.
4. Coalescing must be per-session AtomicBoolean + latest map, not just bounded queue, to cap queued tasks at one per session. Single actor for all sessions means N tasks per publish is a starvation/DoS risk.
5. Type safety of string names: use typed `SignalKey<T>` (like `EnvironmentKey`) or validate types; publish typed. Also avoid `appSignal` (WritableSignal) in v1.
6. `PathlandSession.submit` needs a closed flag + scheduler seam; standalone/SSR sessions need direct execution; exceptions caught/logged. Also re-entrant/actor-thread behavior.
7. Effect exceptions: catch `EffectException`/RuntimeException; don't let a hub task kill the worker. Add telemetry.
8. Tests: actor-thread assertion, coalescing, close-cancel, multi-session, Quarkus background thread, Spring. Distinguish SSR request-thread sessions from live.
9. Non-protocol: no spec changes; update status.md, AGENTS.md bullet, docs guide. Naming.
10. Multi-node: interface boundary; keep canonical map behind a `SignalStore` seam.

Also note: "Acceptance criteria: Works in both Quarkus and Spring Boot test harnesses" — Spring Boot tests live in the starter; Quarkus tests in `pathland-quarkus`.

Also mention that the proposal's `PathlandSession.submit` acceptance "all signal reads, writes, and effect execution occur on the session actor thread" — writing a signal bound via `state()`/`PersistentState` uses a different path; still on actor. Good.

One more subtlety: The hub uses `publish` from Kafka consumer thread. In Quarkus, `@Incoming` may run on event loop; a non-blocking publish must not do heavy work. The design is non-blocking. Good. But `ConcurrentHashMap` updates and `execute` are cheap. Fine.

Another subtlety: A `PathlandSignalHub` bound into the environment must be accessible before the first message? For SSR, the throwaway session's root render uses `app.newRoot()`; if it reads `Environment.value(SESSION_SIGNALS).signal(...)`, the binding is added by `PathlandSession` for both SSR and live. So the hub must be passed to SSR sessions too, or the key must be unbound (then `signal()` fails with NPE). Need to bind a lightweight session-signals for SSR or make `Environment.value` fallback. So `PathlandSession` constructors need the hub, and SSR must supply it. If the hub is per-app, `PathlandApp` provides it. This reinforces the ownership choice.

Also, in SSR, `SessionSignals.signal(name, initial)` must return a signal seeded from the canonical value. If the hub is available, yes. If not (standalone tests), use `initial`. So make a `NoopSessionSignals`/`StandaloneSessionSignals` default.

I'd put `SignalKey` in `dev.pathland.view.core.signal` for DSL friendliness (or server-core? external producers depend on server-core; views depend on view-core. The key must be shared by both. Put it in `view-core` `signal` package so views can define it; server-core depends on view-core already. Good.)
- New `SessionSignals.java` in `view-core` (interface) + implementation.
- `Environment.kt`: add `SESSION_SIGNALS` key (view-core).
- `PathlandApp.java`: optional `default PathlandSignalHub signalHub() { return null; }` OR starter wiring. (Depends on ownership decision.)
- `PathlandTelemetry.java`: add default methods.
- `Emitter`: no changes needed; effects already run on the calling thread.
- `Signals`/`Scheduler`: no changes; maybe add a debug assertion/hook for thread checks? No.

The instruction says don't create docs unless requested; the proposal explicitly asks for docs. But plan mode only; implementation later. Fine.

Open questions:
1. Hub scope: app-owned (`PathlandApp.signalHub()`), registry-owned (host exposes per mount), or process-wide singleton? Recommend app-owned.
2. Typed `SignalKey<T>` vs string names? Recommend typed with string convenience.
3. Do you want `appSignal`/writable canonical in v1 or publish-only? Recommend publish-only.
4. Should `onSession` replay existing sessions? Recommend yes.
5. Is the "arbitrary Runnable submit" public API acceptable, or restrict to hub? Recommend keep but mark low-level.

I should also note the acceptance criterion "no unbounded queues" and "all reads/writes on actor" are correct and testable.

Let me formulate the revised API concretely:

```java
// dev.pathland.server
public interface PathlandSignalHub {
    <T> void publish(SignalKey<T> key, T value);
    <T> Signal<T> appSignal(SignalKey<T> key, T initial); // maybe read-only
    AutoCloseable subscribe(SessionSignalSink sink); // internal-ish
}

public interface PathlandSession {
    void submit(Runnable task);
    SessionSignals signals();
}

public final class PathlandRegistry {
    AutoCloseable onSession(Consumer<PathlandSession> onOpen, Consumer<PathlandSession> onClose);
    void forEachSession(Consumer<PathlandSession> action);
    PathlandSignalHub signalHub(); // if registry-owned
}
```

`SessionSignals`:
```kotlin
interface SessionSignals {
    fun <T> signal(key: SignalKey<T>, initial: T): Signal<T>
    fun submit(task: Runnable)
}
```
`SignalKey<T>`:
```kotlin
class SignalKey<T> private constructor(val name: String) {
    companion object { @JvmStatic fun <T> of(name: String): SignalKey<T> = SignalKey(name) }
}
```
Note: `SignalKey` equality by name? If `of` creates new instances, use name equality; but type params erased. Better a value class with name and equals by name; enforce type on first registration by storing `Class<?>` from `initial`? Can't get generic type. Could require `Class<T> type` in `of`, or accept runtime mismatch and validate `initial.getClass()`. Simpler: `SignalKey.of(name)` and at first signal creation record `initial.getClass()`, then validate subsequent values via `isInstance`. Since generics erase, a mismatch on the external side (`publish(KEY, wrongType)`) is caught at compile-time as long as both use `SignalKey<T>` correctly. The app and producer share the key object. Good enough.

Do we need `appSignal` at all? The app's own code might want to read the canonical value synchronously outside a view (e.g., in a scheduler on a non-actor thread). But that would be a read of a shared signal from outside the actor — fine (no effect), but the `Signal` returned by `appSignal` could be read anywhere; reading records a dependency on the current reactive context, which on a non-actor thread is empty. So it's safe-ish, but values may be slightly stale. For simplicity, drop it or make it a plain `Supplier`/`Signal` of the canonical value. I'll recommend dropping in v1.

Actually the proposal's `appSignal` might be intended for the app to *declare* a signal and the hub to hold its canonical value. The per-session `signal(name, initial)` mirrors it. We can keep an `appSignal` that returns a read-only `Signal<T>` for the canonical value (useful for logging/health). But if it's a `WritableSignal`, external threads can set it directly and bypass the actor. So: read-only or not at all.

Let me finalize.

One more check: `Environment.value` returns `Signal<T>`; if the binding value is the `SessionSignals` object, `toSignal` wraps in a lambda. So `Environment.value(SESSION_SIGNALS)` returns a constant-ish signal. Calling `.signal(...)` on it inside a computed each time returns the same underlying session signal. Good.

Potential subtlety: `Environment.value` uses `VALUES.get()` thread-local; for SSR on request thread, the binding must be set during that render. `Emitter.mount` calls `Environment.within(slot.envScope)` for the root; the root's `envScope` includes the binding from the modifier. Good.

Also note `EnvironmentBinding` is a `ViewModifier`; `PathlandSession` mounts `app.newRoot().modifiers(EnvironmentBinding.with(...))`. Add both keys in one `EnvironmentBinding.with`? The `Config` currently has single `key`/`value`; can't set two keys in one binding. Need either two modifiers or extend Config to support multiple. `modifiers(EnvironmentBinding.with(ACTIVE_PATH...), EnvironmentBinding.with(SESSION_SIGNALS...))` works. Fine.

Now write the answer.

Let me also mention a minor bug-like concern: the proposal says "signal injected into the Pathland environment can physically be set from a consumer thread, but that runs emitter/binding effects on the consumer thread while the session actor may be rendering the same tree." Actually the emitter's node bindings use `Scheduler` global and effects; a write from another thread will flush synchronously on that thread (Scheduler is synchronized, so it won't interleave, but it will run effects on the wrong thread and can interleave with actor tasks at the task boundary; also `ReactiveContext` is thread-local so dependency tracking may be inconsistent). The diagnosis is right; the global `Scheduler` lock prevents data corruption but not the actor contract. Worth noting: the `@Synchronized` scheduler means it's not a raw data race in the JVM-memory sense, but it violates the single-threaded contract and can deadlock/starve? Not deadlock, but effects run off-actor and can observe partial state. I'll phrase precisely: "not necessarily a torn-memory race thanks to the synchronized Scheduler, but a contract violation with real ordering/interleaving hazards and effect execution on the wrong thread." Good nuance.

Also: `Scheduler` is a process-wide static object shared across sessions and SSR. The actor is per registry. So the "single-threaded" claim is actually "serialized by Scheduler lock + actor per registry"; an external write flushes effects on the wrong thread while holding the global lock, potentially blocking the actor. That's a performance/ordering issue. The fix is correct.

questions.question: Where should PathlandSignalHub live for multi-app hosts?

options.label: App-scoped via PathlandApp (Recommended)
options.description: PathlandApp exposes an optional signalHub(); each mounted app owns its own hub and sessions subscribe to their app's hub. Clean isolation for PathlandHost mounts.

options.label: Registry-scoped per mount

options.label: Process-wide singleton
options.description: One hub bean shared by every registry; simplest injection, but signal names must be globally unique across mounted apps or publishes cross apps.

options.label: String names
options.description: Simplest for the Kafka example as written, but mismatched types are only caught at runtime and names are app-global.

options.label: Typed key + String convenience
options.description: Ship SignalKey<T> as the primary API and add a string overload with runtime type validation at first registration.

parts.text: But this seems very broadcast like? For the most part, it would probably a matter of finding the correct session to update a signal for. if a customer has logged in an sees his orders, and then changes his name ad it updates on all his orders. Then only his orders are changes and no one elses.

The user is pushing back: they think the hub design is too broadcast-oriented. The actual common case is targeted updates: "customer changes name → only that customer's sessions/orders update, not everyone's." So we need a routing/selector concept: publish to sessions matching a predicate/key (e.g., user id, tenant id, order id).

This is a very good point. Let me reason through the architecture.

Current proposal: `hub.publish(name, value)` fans out to every session subscribed to that signal name. That's broadcast. The user wants targeted fan-out: only sessions belonging to a customer (or order, tenant, route, etc.).

Key questions:
1. How do we identify sessions/targets? Sessions are keyed by `uiId` (per-connection), with a `stateScope` window id. There's no notion of "user id" or "principal". Need a session attribute / topic / key.
2. How does a view declare its interest? Options:
   - A "channel/topic" per session: `session.subscribe(topic)` derived from app data (e.g., `"customer:" + customerId`). The view declares the topic(s) it cares about; external producer publishes to a topic. Only sessions subscribed to that topic get the update.
   - A per-key hub: `hub.forKey("customer:42").publish(...)`; session signals are scoped by key.
   - A selector/predicate on publish: `hub.publishWhere(s -> s.attribute("customerId").equals(id), name, value)`. This requires session attributes and scans all sessions (O(n) per publish). Fine for moderate n but not ideal; also attributes need a lifecycle.
   - A `SignalKey` with a "scope" part: `SignalKey<Long> CUSTOMER_NAME = SignalKey.scoped("customer.name", CUSTOMER_ID)`. Hmm.

The cleanest server-driven-UI model: **topics (a.k.a. channels/rooms)**. A session subscribes to topics. A publish targets a topic. Only sessions subscribed to that topic receive it.

How does a session subscribe? Either:
- explicitly: `SessionSignals.subscribe("customer:42")` from the app, or
- implicitly via the signal key: `session.signal(CustomerSignals.NAME.with(customerId), initial)` registers the session's interest in that scoped key. Then `hub.publish(CustomerSignals.NAME.with(customerId), value)` only updates sessions that have that scoped key's local signal. This is elegant: the local-signal registry already knows which sessions hold which signal key; publish can look up subscribers by key instead of broadcasting to all sessions.

That is the key insight: **the hub already tracks per-session mirrors keyed by `SignalKey`; it can index by key → set of sessions**. Then `publish(key, value)` targets exactly the sessions that have that key. The "broadcast" only happens for a global key; a per-customer key naturally targets only sessions that created it. No separate subscription API needed.

So the scoped key should carry a dynamic scope. Two designs:

A. `SignalKey<T>` is a constant (name + identity). Scope is a separate parameter:
```java
<T> Signal<T> signal(SignalKey<T> key, Object scope, T initial);
<T> void publish(SignalKey<T> key, Object scope, T value);
```
Where `scope` is the customer/order id. The view calls `session.signal(CustomerSignals.NAME, customerId, initial)`. The producer calls `hub.publish(CustomerSignals.NAME, customerId, newName)`. Hub index key = `(SignalKey, scope)`.

B. `SignalKey<T>` is scoped/factory-generated:
```java
public interface SignalKey<T> { String name(); }
public static <T> ScopedSignalKey<T> scoped(SignalKey<T> base, Object scope);
```
Then `session.signal(CustomerSignals.NAME.scope(customerId), initial)` and `hub.publish(CustomerSignals.NAME.scope(customerId), value)`. This creates a key object per scope; must implement equals/hashCode (base + scope). More allocation, but clear.

C. session attributes + selector:
```java
session.attribute("customerId", id); // set at login/SSR
hub.publishWhere(s -> id.equals(s.attribute("customerId")), KEY, value);
```
This is "find the correct session" but requires scanning and a mutable attribute bag. It also doesn't naturally handle multiple sessions per customer unless filtered. It's more like a query API. Could be useful for admin cases ("drop all sessions for tenant X") but not as the primary.

I think A or B is best. The "scope" is the routing key. The hub maintains `ConcurrentHashMap<ScopedKey, Map<SessionMirror, Signal>>` or `Map<ScopedKey, Set<SessionSignals>>`. Actually simpler: each session has `Map<ScopedKey, WritableSignal>`; the hub has `Map<ScopedKey, Set<SessionMirror>>` (subscriber index). On `signal(key, scope, initial)`, register `(key, scope) -> session` and create the local signal seeded from the canonical value for that scoped key. On `publish`, look up the subscriber set and schedule only those. This is targeted, O(subscribers), no broadcast.

This also solves the new-session seeding: the canonical map is keyed by `(key, scope)`, and the view's `signal(key, scope, initial)` seeds from it. Cleanup: when a session closes, remove it from all scoped subscriber sets. If a view stops caring about a scope (e.g., navigates away), the local signal is created but never read; we may want to garbage-collect scoped entries when no session holds them. Could keep a weak reference or clean up when the last session unsubscribes; but for a long-lived app with many customer ids, the canonical map could grow unbounded. Need a lifecycle:
- The canonical value for a scoped key is needed only to seed newly opened sessions. How long do we keep it? Options: TTL (e.g., reset when no subscribers and no recent publish), or re-fetch from a backing store on new session, or keep a bounded LRU. For ephemeral signals like "events consumed", maybe the canonical value is a counter that grows; keeping it is fine but unbounded by customer count.
- Better: distinguish "global app signals" (single canonical) from "scoped signals" (per entity). Scoped canonical values should be treated as a cache with TTL/LRU, or the app should treat them as derived from the entity state. If a new session subscribes to `customer:42` after all prior sessions closed, it should get the current name — but where from? If the hub evicted it, it needs a loader/initial. The view's `initial` is the fallback, but it may be stale. So provide an optional "loader" or let the app re-publish on subscription (`onSubscribe` callback). Alternatively, the app can publish to the scope when the entity changes and accept that a new session with no live holder seeds from its `initial` (which the app can compute per-session, e.g., from a DB read in `body()`). Actually the view can compute the initial from server data (it's a server-side render), so `initial` is fresh at session creation. The hub's canonical is only needed for sessions that opened before a publish but haven't read the signal yet; and for live sessions the publish updates them. So maybe the canonical map for scoped signals is just "latest published since process start", and `initial` is the source of truth for a new session. That's a reasonable contract: scoped signals are ephemeral deltas; the app must supply a correct initial per session. Document it.

Hmm, but then a session that subscribes *after* a publish but before rendering (the race) could read `initial` instead of the latest. The canonical map prevents that. TTL/LRU would mitigate unbounded growth. Or use the `onSession`/subscribe hook to re-publish current entity state. For a first version, a bounded LRU on scoped canonical entries (e.g., 10k) with metrics is fine.

Another important point: the user says "if a customer has logged in and sees his orders, and then changes his name and it updates on all his orders. Then only his orders are changed and no one else's." Note "all his orders" — there may be multiple sessions/tabs/devices for the same customer, and/or multiple order views within one session. Scoped key `(CUSTOMER_NAME, customerId)` targets all sessions subscribed to that customer. Within a session, one local signal can drive multiple views (they all call `signal(key, customerId, initial)` and get the same underlying signal). Good.

But how does the session know the customer id? The view calls `signal(KEY, customerId, initial)`; the customer id comes from the view's data (e.g., the order's customer). If a session has multiple orders (maybe different customers? usually same customer), each order view subscribes to its customer. Fine.

There's also the "user identity / auth" angle: if the app uses a session principal, you might want `session.principal` or `session.attribute("customerId")` and a `hub.publishToCustomer(id, ...)` convenience. But the scoped-signal approach already encodes targeting in the view's subscription; no server-side notion of a user is needed. That's good because Pathland core has no auth model. The app can build a thin wrapper:
```java
hub.publish(CustomerSignals.NAME, customerId, newName);
```
or `customerHub.publishName(customerId, newName)`.

Also the user says "finding the correct session to update a signal for." This suggests a **session lookup by key** (like `registry.sessionsFor(key)`) rather than broadcast. The scoped-signal index is exactly that: finding sessions subscribed to a key. But sometimes external code knows the session id (e.g., from a websocket connection, or state store) and wants `registry.session(id).submit(...)`. That's the direct path. We should expose both:
- targeted by scope: `hub.publish(key, scope, value)` (index lookup),
- direct by session: `session.submit(...)` / `registry.session(id)` if needed.

The current `onSession`/`forEachSession` is more like an observer/listener API for the hub to subscribe, not necessarily public broadcast. The public API is `publish(key, scope, value)` which is targeted. So the user's concern is addressed by adding scope to the key/publish.

```java
    public static final SignalKey<String> NAME = SignalKey.of("name");

session.signal(CUSTOMER.customer(customerId).key(NAME), initial)
```

We need to define the scope type. `Object`/`String`/`long`? Use `Object` with proper equals/hashCode, or a typed `SignalScope` (name + id). For type safety, `<S> SignalKey<T>` with a scope type? Could be:
```java
public final class SignalKey<T> { ... }
// scope is any value with stable equals/hashCode, usually a String/Long
<T> Signal<T> signal(SignalKey<T> key, Object scope, T initial);
<T> void publish(SignalKey<T> key, Object scope, T value);
```

And a global scope constant `SignalScope.GLOBAL` / `null`. For the broadcast case (global counter), use `SignalScope.GLOBAL`. This unifies both.

Naming: maybe `SignalKey<T>` + `scope` overloads; and `publish(key, value)` delegates to `publish(key, GLOBAL, value)`. Good.

Now the canonical map keyed by `(SignalKey, scope)`: a record `ScopedKey(SignalKey<?> key, Object scope)` with equals/hashCode. Subscriber index `Map<ScopedKey, Set<SessionMirror>>`.

Per-session `SessionSignals`:
- `signal(key, scope, initial)`: compute `scoped = scopedKey(key, scope)`; local map `Map<ScopedKey, WritableSignal<?>>`; if absent, create with canonical value if present else initial; register subscription in hub; return it.
- Important: `signal()` is called during render; it must not mutate shared hub state off-actor. It runs on the actor for live sessions, so fine. For SSR, it runs on the request thread; it must not register as a subscriber (or must be a read-only/throwaway session). Distinguish via `subscribe` flag. Seeding from the hub's canonical map (a ConcurrentHashMap) is thread-safe read.

Now targeted publish:

```java
hub.publish(NAME, customerId, newName);
// lookup subscribers for (NAME, customerId), schedule each mirror's flush
```
Only the customer's sessions update. 

What about "all his orders": if each order view subscribes to `(CUSTOMER_NAME, customerId)`, both update. If the orders are in different sessions, both sessions' mirrors update. Good.

What about a "customer's orders list changes" event with an order id scope? Same pattern.

The subscription is created when the view renders the signal; if a session navigates away, the local signal may remain registered (subscriber index stale) unless the view unsubscribes. The emitter destroys the component slot and its tracked signals; but the `SessionSignals` local signal is not tied to a component's lifecycle because it's created in `body()` and not destroyed automatically. This is a **resource leak / over-subscription** concern:

Given the current architecture, over-subscription is a real concern for high-cardinality scopes (customer id, order id). We should address it in the plan:
- Keep a per-session map of scoped signals with a **last-read timestamp** updated on `get()`? Too expensive on every get.
- Or a bounded LRU per session (e.g., 1024 scoped signals) and unsubscribe on eviction. This bounds subscription count per session; a view that still reads an evicted signal would recreate it (and re-seed). But the returned `Signal` reference held by the view would be stale if evicted? The view re-runs `body()` and calls `signal()` again, getting a new mirror. If the view holds the old signal in a field, it breaks. But the recommended pattern is to call `signal()` in `body()` each render; the emitter rerenders on changes. If a signal is evicted and recreated, a computed holding the old signal won't update. Hmm. Need careful lifecycle.
- Better: tie scoped signals to the **component slot** lifetime. The emitter already tracks `bindings`/`nodeBindings` and destroys them. If `signal()` is called during a component render, we can associate the signal with the current component's slot/effect and subscribe while the component is mounted. But the signal may be shared across components (same key+scope) and across renders. Ref-count subscriptions per session: each component that calls `signal()` increments a ref count, and slot destruction decrements. This is doable if we expose a `SignalLease`/`Scope` with close, or integrate with `Emitter`'s component lifecycle. But it's more invasive.

Maybe simpler for v1: treat `SessionSignals` as session-scoped, not component-scoped. Over-subscription is bounded by the number of distinct (key, scope) pairs a session ever reads. For typical apps (customer has a handful of orders), that's fine. Add a configurable per-session subscription cap and an LRU to bound it. Document that. Or provide `session.signals().release(key, scope)` for manual cleanup.

But the user's framing suggests they mostly want targeted routing, not necessarily lifecycle perfection. Let me present the options and recommend:
- Targeted publish via scoped keys (primary).
- Subscription lifecycle: session-scoped for v1; optionally bind to component slot later. Add a cap/TTL to avoid unbounded growth.
- Direct session targeting: `registry.session(uiId)`/`onSession` for cases where you know the session (e.g., a websocket connection maps to a user), with `session.submit`.

There is a slot lifecycle (`destroySlotTree`), but `SessionSignals.signal()` is just returning a signal, not an effect. We could add a "slot lease" mechanism: if `signal()` is called during a render, register the scoped key with the current slot (`ViewSlot`), and on slot destroy, decrement/release. But `signal()` is in view-core (the session signals impl) and the emitter's `ViewSlot` is in engine (view-core module, package `dev.pathland.view.engine`). Could add an `Emitter.current()` / `ReactiveContext` integration. But it's more invasive. For v1, session-scoped with a cap/TTL is simpler. I'll mention the option.

Wait, the user's main concern is broadcast vs targeted. Let me not over-focus on lifecycle. But I should mention the over-subscription issue because it's directly caused by the targeted approach (an ever-growing set of scopes). Keep it as a design note and recommend a bounded per-session scope map + optional release.

Let me also consider: perhaps the best API is to make the **scope part of the signal key at declaration**, e.g. a "family" key:

```java
SignalFamily<CustomerId, String> NAME = SignalFamily.of("customer.name");
session.signal(NAME, customerId, initial);
hub.publish(NAME, customerId, value);
```

But a simple `SignalKey<T>` + `scope` object achieves the same. Use `Object scope` and document. Maybe add a typed helper `SignalScope<K>`? Not needed.

Now, what about the "canonical value" and targeted routing: canonical map keyed by `(key, scope)`. For customer names, unbounded growth if many customers. Need eviction. Options:
- TTL-based `ConcurrentHashMap` with expiry (e.g., 5–30 min) and LRU cap.
- Or don't keep canonical for scoped signals; instead require the view's `initial` to be fresh (it's server-rendered) and rely on live updates. Then a new session opened after a publish but before it reads could miss an update; but the view's `initial` (from DB) is fresh, so no problem. Actually the user's name-change example: the DB is updated, then `hub.publish` notifies live sessions. A new session opened after the DB update reads the fresh name from DB → correct. A new session opened *before* the DB update gets the old value, then the publish updates it. So the canonical map isn't strictly needed if the app's `initial` is the source of truth! The only race is: DB updated, publish happens, and a session was created between the DB update and the publish — its `initial` read from DB (fresh) is correct anyway. Or DB not yet updated and publish happens? Then the session seeds from DB (old) and gets the publish later if subscribed before the publish. If it subscribes after the publish, it missed it; but its `initial` from DB is old (if DB update after publish). This is a consistency race inherent to the app's write order (publish after commit). So the canonical map helps bridge publish-to-late-subscriber. But it duplicates entity state in memory. A TTL/LRU is needed.

Alternatively, the hub can support a **loader** on first subscription: `session.signal(key, scope, initial)` where `initial` is already fresh. Then no canonical needed. But a session that is already live and re-renders after a publish (but its local signal was created before) gets the update via subscription. Fine.

Hmm, the canonical map is useful for "global" signals (counters). For scoped entity signals, the initial from the entity is authoritative. Maybe the design should distinguish:
- **Global keys** (`scope = GLOBAL`): canonical map, broadcast to all subscribed sessions. E.g., "events consumed".
- **Scoped keys**: canonical map optional/bounded; the view's `initial` is the source of truth; live updates are deltas.

For simplicity, keep a bounded canonical map for both, with eviction. Document that the app should supply a correct per-session `initial` for scoped signals.

Actually, wait. There's a subtle issue with `initial` and re-render: `signal(key, scope, initial)` is called on every render. If the local signal exists, the `initial` is ignored. parts.text:
Great. `Text(Signal<String>)` exists, `Signal<T>.value` extension exists (`.value`), `map` exists. So DX can be:

```kotlin
val name = subscribe(Customer.name, customerId, initialName)
Text(name)                       // Text(Signal<String>) overload
Text(orders.map { "${it.size} orders" })  // computed
```

Or use `.value`:
```kotlin
Text("Customer: ${name.value}")
```
Wait `Text` with a string would not be reactive; `.value` read during body would subscribe the component (body is tracked). Yes, reading a signal in `body()` tracks the component slot, so `Text("... ${name.value}")` re-renders the component on change (coarser than binding). Better to pass the signal to `Text(name)` for fine-grained binding. But DX-wise both readable.

Now, the subscription API. To maximize DX:
- Define `Topic<T>` with an `invoke` operator or extension:
  ```kotlin
  val name = subscribe(Customer.name, customerId, initialName)
  ```
  Top-level `subscribe` in `dev.pathland.view.dsl`. `Customer.name` is `Topic<String>`.
- Or `Customer.name.subscribe(customerId, initialName)`.
  Reads: "Customer.name subscribed for customerId with initialName". Nice.
  But a top-level `subscribe` avoids importing extension? You need to import `dev.pathland.view.dsl.subscribe`; the topic class maybe in domain package. Actually if the user defines `Customer.name` in their app, and calls `.subscribe`, they need the extension imported. The top-level `subscribe` also needs import. Fine.
- For the publisher, `hub.publish(Customer.name, customerId, updatedName)`.

Maybe make the subscription API mirror `subscribe(topic, subject) { initial }`? No.

Could define `Topic<T>` as:
```kotlin
class Topic<T>(val name: String) {
    fun subscribe(subject: Any, initial: T): Signal<T> = ...
}
```
Then the topic itself knows how to subscribe (calls the environment). But `Topic` lives in view-core; it can call `Environment.value(SUBSCRIPTIONS).get()`. That's clean DX: `Customer.name.subscribe(customerId, initialName)`. And for publishing, `hub.publish(Customer.name, customerId, value)`. Or the topic can have `publish`? It would need the hub, which is server-side. Could have `Topic.publish` only in server context—not clean. Keep `hub.publish`.

Maybe the best DX is a `Subscription<T>` value that bundles topic + subject + initial:
```kotlin
val name = watched(Customer.name, customerId, initialName)
```
No.

Let me consider naming: "subscribe" is clear. The user said "some kind of subscription system." So `subscribe` is the verb. `Customer.name.subscribe(customerId, initialName)` reads well.

But there's a subtlety: `subscribe` returns a signal but is called during `body()`. If called in a field initializer (not body), the environment may not be set. The recommended pattern is in `body()`. The existing `state()` is a protected method in Component and works in field initializers? It binds later. For subscriptions, we could support field initialization by deferring resolution until first `get()` (like `EnvironmentSignal`). Then:
```kotlin
class CustomerOrdersView(val customerId: Long, val initialName: String) : Component() {
    private val name = Customer.name.subscribe(customerId, initialName)
    override fun body() = VStack { Text(name) }
}
```
This is the best DX: declare subscriptions as fields, use them in `body()`/`computed`. Can we make it work? `Topic.subscribe` could return a lazy `Signal<T>` that on first `get()` resolves the session subscription via `Environment.value(SUBSCRIPTIONS).get()`. But the subscription must be registered with the hub when? On first `get()`, which happens during render (body/Text binding), so the environment is set. That's fine. But if the signal is never read, no registration. Good. However, registering during a `get()` inside a computed/effect is a side effect (fine). But the first `get()` might happen when `Text` computes its initial untracked value during render; the environment is set. Good.
- But `Environment.value(SUBSCRIPTIONS).get()` inside `Signal.get()` each time is a thread-local lookup; cheap. Or cache after first resolution.

It's the right level of abstraction: one factory, one return type, no new ceremony. It also reads naturally in both places:

```kotlin

// In the publisher
```
