 # pathland-view-core (JVM engine + DSL) — implementation status
 
 **Last updated:** November 7, 2026
 
 The shared, framework-agnostic JVM engine, runtime and authoring DSL for the
 Pathland protocol, written entirely in Kotlin. It owns the `View` SPI and shared
 authoring vocabulary, the retained-tree diff emitter,
 signals/computed/effects, the wire codec, router, cross-platform state, JNA ring
 interop, and the `dev.pathland.view.dsl` SwiftUI-shaped builders/modifiers.
 Server and renderer modules depend on this one module; Java hosts consume the
 Kotlin-authored views through JVM interop.
 
 ## Implemented
 
 - **Protocol** (`dev.pathland.view.core.protocol`): `Components`, `Properties`,
   `Commands` (incl. `SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT`), `Categories`, `ValueTypes`, `Opcode`,
   `ValueEncoder`, `WireValue`, `TokenPath`.
 - **Attributed text** (`dev.pathland.view.core.AttributedString`): pure-Kotlin
   model + range-tracking builder (Kotlin char indices → UTF-8 byte offsets) and
   payload encode/decode; `Text(AttributedString)` / `Text(Signal<AttributedString>)`
   emit `SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT` through the emitter and both sinks.
 - **Built-in inline Markdown**: `Text("...")` parses the v1 subset by default
   (`**bold**`/`__bold__`, `*italic*`/`_italic_`, `` `code` ``,
   `~~strikethrough~~`, `[label](url)`); `markdown = false` renders literal text.
   `dev.pathland.markdown.Markdown` is now a **pure-Java parser** (no native
   library, so it runs on every platform and under GraalVM native-image); it is a
   behavioural port of the Rust `pathland-markdown` crate (pre-scan + bounded
   cache). The Rust crate remains the parser for the Rust DSL and non-JVM hosts.
   Plain results use the compact `SET_TEXT` path; rich results emit
   `SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT`. Reactive `Text(Signal<String>)` parses on change.
 - **Signals** (`dev.pathland.view.core.signal`): `signal`/`state`/`computed`/
   `effect`/`untracked`, synchronous glitch-free flush, equality suppression, error
   caching/retry, circular-dependency detection, and a thread-safe global
   `Scheduler`. `Signals.state` binds to the ambient session `PersistentState`
   during a component render.
+- **Topic subscriptions** (`dev.pathland.view.core.subscription`): a strongly
+  typed, always-scoped `Topic<T, S>` and the DSL `topic(key, subject, initial)`
+  (also `Signals.topic`). Returns a normal `Signal<T>` backed by a session-local
+  mirror; the server runtime registers it with the app's hub and applies
+  published values on the session actor. `SessionContext` (thread-local, installed
+  by `PathlandSession` around every actor task) also exposes `unsubscribe` and
+  `submit`. Resolution is lazy when a root view's field initializer runs before
+  the context is installed.
 - **State** (`dev.pathland.view.core.state`): `PersistentState`, untyped
   `StateStore`, in-memory store and provider. Kotlin `Component` state delegates
   bind directly before `body()`; the Java `State` field/binder machinery and
   annotation processor are removed.
 - **Transport** (`dev.pathland.view.core.transport`): `ProtocolFrame`,
   `FrameCodec`, `Event`, `EnvironmentData`, `OpcodeSink`, `FrameOpcodeSink`.
   **Hardened (issue #63)**: `FrameCodec.parse` reads the attacker-controlled
   `opcodeCount`/`stringsLen` as unsigned `Long` values and validates them
   against the actual message length before allocating; string offsets are
   bounds-checked (`Parsed.stringAt`). A declared `opcodeCount` that overflows
   `Int` arithmetic now throws instead of triggering an OOM allocation.
 - **Router** (`dev.pathland.view.core.router`): `Route`, `RouteTable`, `Router`,
   `Navigation`, `NavigationContainer`, `NavigationIntent`, `Params`, `Chrome`,
   `NavOp`. `NavigationLink` and the navigation helpers live in the Kotlin DSL.
 - **JNA interop** (`dev.pathland.view.core.ffm`): lazy `PathlandCore` binding and
   `RingOpcodeSink` over `libpathland_core`.
 - **Emitter** (`dev.pathland.view.engine`): `Emitter`, `PathlandNode`, `ViewSlot`,
   `RenderResult`, `InputDispatcher`, `ReactiveValues`, `DateInput`, `MediaInput`.
   Implements mount/id assignment, diff-based reactive emission, node-level binding
   effects, structural reconciliation, fit/media/navigation routing, and the
   zero-opcode unchanged recompute contract. A replaced child is relinked to its
   real parent (not the tree root), so a `SIZE_THAT_FITS` swap cannot detach a
   pinned root `MEDIA_CONTROLLER` or drop its media routing. Registered `MediaController`s are
   projected as pinned, non-visual root children; `unregisterMediaController`
   removes them without touching the app tree.
 - **Shared SPI/values** (`dev.pathland.view.core`): `View`, `ViewModifier`,
   `Configurable`, `ChildrenView`, `Modified`, `ViewBuilder`,
   `Environment*`, `Platform`, `Theme*`, `MediaController`, `WindowMetadata`,
   `ProxyConfig`, `Color`, `Length`, shared enums, style protocols, and modifier
   wrappers.
 - **Protocol manifest validation** (`ProtocolManifestTest`): the hand-written
   protocol constants (`Components`, `Properties`, `Commands`, `Categories`,
   `ValueTypes`) are checked against `spec/protocol.tsv` — including no extra
   public numeric constants and the full `ValueTypes.forProperty` mapping. No
   Java source is generated.
 - **Shared engine traces**: the Kotlin DSL tests run the mount/text/property
   scenarios against the Rust-emitted PLPL fixtures under `spec/engine-traces/`,
   byte-for-byte. The canonical order lives in `spec/ENGINE.md`.
 - **Tests**: `pathland-view-core` owns the signal, state, frame-codec, and
   protocol-manifest tests; Kotlin DSL tests exercise the emitter end-to-end, and
   the server/HTML/desktop consumers cover their integration paths.
 
 ## Authoring DSL (`dev.pathland.view.dsl`)
 
 - **SwiftUI-shaped builders**: `Text` (plain, `Signal<String>`, or
   `AttributedString` / `Signal<AttributedString>`), `Image`, `Icon`, `Color`,
   `Rectangle`, `Circle`, `Ellipse`, `Capsule`, `RoundedRectangle`, `Shape`,
   `Divider`, `Spacer`, `ProgressView`, `Gauge`, `Label`, `Group`.
 - **Containers**: `VStack`, `HStack`, `ZStack`, `Grid`, `GridRow`, `ScrollView`,
   `LazyVStack`, `LazyHStack`, `LazyVGrid`, `LazyHGrid`, `ViewThatFits`/`Fit`,
   `ProxyView`, `ForEach`.
 - **Controls**: `Button` (title or label subtree), `TextField`, `SecureField`,
   `TextEditor`, `Toggle`, `Slider`, `Stepper`, `DatePicker`, `Picker`, `Menu`,
   `ColorPicker`.
 - **Automatic child collection**: `VStack { Text("a"); Text("b") }` needs no
   `.children(...)`. A custom `Component` constructed inline in a block
   auto-registers; a view stored as a field is added explicitly with `+field`.
 - **Scope isolation** (`@PathlandDsl`): every view builder lambda takes a
   `PathlandScope` receiver, and `PathlandScope`, `Navigation.Builder`, and the
   modifier/style `Config` receivers carry the same `@DslMarker`. An outer
   router/config receiver therefore cannot be captured implicitly inside a
   nested view builder (e.g. `fallback(...)` inside `VStack { }` is a compile
   error). Child collection itself is unchanged — the thread-local `ViewScopes`
   stack still drives auto-registration.
 - **Signals**: `signal`, `computed`, `constant`, `effect`, `untracked`,
-  `Signal<T>.value`, `WritableSignal<T>.value`, `Signal<T>.map`, `readonly`.
+  `topic(key, subject, initial)`, `Signal<T>.value`, `WritableSignal<T>.value`,
+  `Signal<T>.map`, `readonly`.
 - **Modifier sugar**: `.padding`, `.frame`, `.offset`, `.position`, `.fixedSize`,
   layout priority/z-index/aspect ratio, the full text-formatting surface,
   foreground/background/border/corner radius/shadow, visual effects, transforms,
   visibility/disabled/hit-testing, accessibility, tap/pointer events,
   environment binding, styles, window metadata, and navigation intents.
 - **Persisted state**: `Component` base class + `val count by state(0)`
   (auto-keyed by property name) or `state(0, "key")`; a `mutableState(0)` signal
   form for two-way controls.
 - **Reactive bodies**: plain `if`/`when`/`for` in `body()`; `ForEach` over a static
   list or `Signal<List<T>>` with row-scoped child collection.
 - **Navigation**: `navigator { route(...) }`, `NavigationStack`, `NavigationLink`,
   `isActive`, and `.navigate`/`.push`/`.replace` intents.
 - **Media**: `Video(controller)` stays where the app places it; audio remains
   view-less. `controller.register()` projects a controller at the root.
 - **Naming**: the composite base is `Component` (renamed from `KotlinView` now
   that the Java DSL is gone); see #174.
 - **Java hosting**: a Java Spring Boot / Quarkus app mounts a Kotlin view through
   the Java-friendly `PathlandApp` functional interface
   (`return () -> MusicPlayerView.make();`). Kotlin roots expose public
   constructors and/or `@JvmStatic make(...)` factories.
 
 ## Package boundary
 
 - `pathland-view-core` is one Maven module: `core`/`engine`/`dsl` are logical
   subpackages inside it, with a few deliberate intra-module references
   (`Color`/`MediaController`/`Modified` materialize `PathlandNode`). Splitting
   them into separate artifacts would require a node SPI first.
 - Production runtimes/renderers (`pathland-server-core`,
   `pathland-render-html`) depend on this module. Framework starters remain
   DSL-neutral at compile time; they mount Kotlin-authored fixture views in test
   scope.

fun text(value: String): View = Text(value)

fun counterApp(): View {
    val count = signal(0)
    return VStack(spacing = 8f) {
        Text("Kotlin-authored view")
        Button("Bump") { count.value = count.value + 1 }
        Text(computed { "n=${count.value}" })
    }
}

/**

 * node 2 is its dynamic `n=<count>` label.

fun counterProbe(): View {
    val count = signal(0)
    return Button(
        title = computed { "n=${count.value}" },
        action = { count.value = count.value + 1 },
    )

package dev.pathland.view.core.subscription

/**
 * A strongly typed, always-scoped subscription key.
 *
 * [T] is the published payload type and [S] is the subject (the thing the
 * subscription is about — a customer id, order id, tenant, conversation, …).
 * Both are checked at compile time by [subscribe] and
 * `PathlandSignalHub.publish`.
 *
 * Identity is by [name] (not by instance), so a topic declared once and shared
 * across modules — or across a process boundary — resolves to the same
 * subscription stream. Two topics with the same name must therefore carry the
 * same payload and subject types; declare each topic once in a shared constant
 * object.
 */
class Topic<T, S> @JvmOverloads constructor(val name: String) {

    override fun equals(other: Any?): Boolean =
        this === other || (other is Topic<*, *> && other.name == name)

    override fun hashCode(): Int = name.hashCode()

    override fun toString(): String = "Topic($name)"

    companion object {
        /** A topic named [name] with payload type [T] and subject type [S]. */
        @JvmStatic
        fun <T, S> of(name: String): Topic<T, S> = Topic(name)
    }
}

# pathland-spring-boot-starter — implementation status

**Last updated:** November 6, 2026

Spring Boot auto-configuration for Pathland: SSR at any path, live deltas over each
app's reserved `/{base}/ws`, per-session state. Adding the starter dependency + a
`PathlandApp` bean gives a running app; `MountedApp` beans host more apps at their own
subpaths (the BFF layout).

## Implemented

- **Security hardening (issue #63)**: the WebSocket handlers no longer hardcode
  `setAllowedOrigins("*")`. The default is Spring's same-origin handshake check
  (the WebSocket CSRF control); cross-origin hosts must be listed explicitly in
  `pathland.allowed-origins` (comma-separated). The handshake `wid` is validated
  by server-core (`WindowIds`). SSR inherits SRI (`integrity="sha384-…"`) from
  `PathlandSession`. CSP/security headers and transport limits are documented in
  `docs/HARDENING.md` (Quarkus supplies secure defaults; Spring apps add them
  through Spring Security/server configuration).
- **Hosted deployments work by default (issue #45 follow-up)**: a
  lowest-precedence `EnvironmentPostProcessor` contributes
  `server.forward-headers-strategy=framework`, so a TLS-terminating PaaS gets a
  correct WebSocket same-origin check and external SSR canonical URL with zero
  configuration. An explicit `server.forward-headers-strategy` in application
  config always wins (`ForwardedHeaderOverrideTest` pins this).
- **Java host / Kotlin views**: `KotlinViewMountTest` proves a Java-only
  `@SpringBootApplication` bean returning `PathlandApp` mounts a Kotlin-authored
  fixture view, renders it through SSR, and receives a live signal delta.

- **Crawler endpoints**: `/robots.txt` (text/plain) and `/sitemap.xml` (application/xml) are real routes before the SPA catch-all, so Lighthouse does not parse the HTML shell as robots.txt.
- **SEO document head (issue #45)**: the SSR controller derives the canonical
  URL from the request and passes host-default `PageMetadata` to the registry;
  `PathlandApp.pageMetadata(...)` may override it per route before the first
  paint. Canonical/OG/Twitter/JSON-LD are on by default and configurable via
  `pathland.seo.{enabled,site-name,image,og-type,twitter-card,twitter-site,structured-data}`.

- **`PathlandAutoConfiguration`** (`@AutoConfiguration`, `@EnableWebSocket` since Spring
  Boot 3.5 no longer auto-enables it) + `META-INF/spring/…/AutoConfiguration.imports`:
  - default `StateStore` bean (`@ConditionalOnMissingBean` — Redis-or-in-memory),
  - `PathlandHost` bean (shut down with the context): every `MountedApp` bean plus the
    lone `PathlandApp` bean mounted at `/` (unless an explicit `MountedApp` claims the
    root). Without any app the host is empty and the starter is inert.
  - a `WebSocketConfigurer` registering **one handler per app** at its framework base
    (`/_pathland/ws` for the root, `/{mount}/_pathland/ws` otherwise). Each connection
    gets a fresh `uiId` (its UI model) + the client's `wid` (per-window state scope)
    from the WS `?wid=` query param (kept in `sessionStorage`, never in the page URL),
  - `PathlandIndexController` (SSR catch-all dispatching to the longest-mount app with
    the prefix stripped + a framework static controller serving the bundle + asset mount
    from `classpath:/static/_pathland/**` at both `/_pathland/**` and `/{app}/_pathland/**`;
    the more-specific mapping beats `/{*path}`, and the `!Upgrade` header excludes WS).

input.content:
# External UI updates with topic subscriptions

Pathland signals are single-threaded by contract: reads, writes, and effects run
on the session's actor. Background work (Kafka/SmallRye `@Incoming` consumers,
scheduled jobs, database notifications, other transports) runs on its own
threads, so it must not set a view's signal directly.

Topic subscriptions are the supported bridge. A view subscribes to a
**strongly typed, always-scoped** topic and gets a normal `Signal<T>`; external
code publishes a value for the same `(topic, subject)` pair from any thread, and
only the sessions subscribed to that pair update. The runtime applies the value
on each session's actor, so the existing effect/delta path is unchanged.

## 1. Declare the topic once

A `Topic<T, S>` carries the payload type `T` and the subject type `S`. Topic
identity is its name, so the view and the publisher share the same constant.

```kotlin
object CustomerTopics {
    val NAME: Topic<String, Long> = Topic.of("customer.name")
    val ORDERS: Topic<List<Order>, Long> = Topic.of("customer.orders")
}
```

```java
public final class CustomerTopics {
    public static final Topic<String, Long> NAME = Topic.of("customer.name");
    public static final Topic<List<Order>, Long> ORDERS = Topic.of("customer.orders");

    private CustomerTopics() {}
}
```

## 2. Subscribe in a view

```kotlin
class CustomerOrdersView(
    private val customerId: Long,
    private val initialName: String,
    private val initialOrders: List<Order>,
) : Component() {

    private val name = topic(CustomerTopics.NAME, customerId, initialName)
    private val orders = topic(CustomerTopics.ORDERS, customerId, initialOrders)

    override fun body(): View = VStack(spacing = 8) {
        Text(name)                          // Signal<String>
        ForEach(orders) { OrderCard(it) }   // Signal<List<Order>>
    }
}
```

`topic(...)` returns a regular `Signal<T>`, so `Text(signal)`,
`ForEach(signal)`, `signal.map { }`, and `computed { }` all work. Subscribing is
idempotent per `(topic, subject)` within a session; repeated calls return the
same local signal.

Passing the wrong subject or payload type is a compile error: `NAME` requires a
`Long` subject and a `String` value.

## 3. Publish from any thread

The starter produces a `PathlandSignalHub` bean for the root mount (use
`PathlandHost.signalHub(mount)` in a multi-app host). Publishing is
non-blocking.

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public class CustomerConsumers {

    @Inject PathlandSignalHub hub;

    @Incoming("customer-name-changed")
    void onNameChanged(CustomerNameChanged event) {
        hub.publish(CustomerTopics.NAME, event.customerId(), event.name());
    }
}
```

Only sessions that subscribed to `(customer.name, event.customerId())` are
updated. Two customers, two sessions: publishing customer 42's name never
touches customer 43.

## Semantics

- **Scoped, not broadcast.** The hub looks up subscribers by
  `(topic.name, subject)`. There is no global publish path.
- **Actor-confined.** Published values are applied on the session actor, so all
  signal reads/writes/effects keep the single-threaded contract.
- **Latest wins.** Publishes are coalesced per session: at most one drain task is
  scheduled, and only the newest value per subscription is applied. A hot
  producer cannot flood the actor.
- **`initial` seeds the signal.** A new session renders current data from its own
  source; subsequent changes arrive through `publish`. Late subscribers do not
  receive historical values.
- **Session-scoped lifetime.** Subscriptions end when the session closes.
  `SessionContext.current()?.unsubscribe(topic, subject)` is available for dynamic
  subjects; SSR sessions subscribe for the first paint but do not register with
  the hub.
- **Multi-app isolation.** Each mounted app has its own hub; `/` and `/billing`
  never see each other's topics.

## Notes

- Declare a topic once and share the constant. The topic name is the wire
  identity (a future Redis fan-out can route on it); two topics with the same
  name must carry the same types.
- The subject should be immutable with stable `equals`/`hashCode` — an id, a
  value class, or a record.
- For an app-wide stream, use an explicit singleton subject
  (`object GlobalSubject`) as the `S` type; every subscription is still scoped.
- If you need a lower-level escape hatch, `PathlandSession.submit(Runnable)` and
  `SessionContext.current()?.submit { }` run work on the session actor.

input.newString:
- **Signals** (`dev.pathland.view.core.signal`): `signal`/`state`/`computed`/
  `effect`/`untracked`, synchronous glitch-free flush, equality suppression, error
  caching/retry, circular-dependency detection, and a thread-safe global
  `Scheduler`. `Signals.state` binds to the ambient session `PersistentState`
  during a component render.
- **Topic subscriptions** (`dev.pathland.view.core.subscription`): a strongly
  typed, always-scoped `Topic<T, S>` and the DSL `topic(key, subject, initial)`
  (also `Signals.topic`). Returns a normal `Signal<T>` backed by a session-local
  mirror; the server runtime registers it with the app's hub and applies
  published values on the session actor. `SessionContext` (thread-local, installed
  by `PathlandSession` around every actor task) also exposes `unsubscribe` and
  `submit`. Resolution is lazy when a root view's field initializer runs before
  the context is installed.

parts.text:
One concern: In the constructor, we push the session context, then `applyEnvironment` is called, which calls `runWithContext` and nested push. Fine.

Another concern: `PathlandSession.submit` catches only `RejectedExecutionException`; the registry's `execute` catches it internally, so nothing propagates. Fine.

Another concern: `PathlandSession.submit` uses `scheduler.execute` with the registry's `execute`, which runs the task on the actor and drops if `shuttingDown`. Good.

Another concern: `PathlandSession` constructor now sets `closed` false by default.

Another: `dispatch(byte[])` calls `dispatch(FrameCodec.decodeEvents(message))`; the decode happens on the caller thread (registry actor) outside the context, but it's just decoding. Fine.

Now, one subtle issue: The `SessionContext` thread-local is pushed in `applyEnvironment` and `dispatch`, etc. But the `PathlandRegistry` also calls `session.resync()` inside an actor task; `resync` pushes context. Good. `session.close()` doesn't push context; `subscriptions.close` doesn't need it.

Potential issue with SSR: `PathlandRegistry.renderHtml` constructs the session with `scheduler=null` -> `Runnable::run` and `hub=null`. The constructor pushes context; `app.newRoot()` field-based `topic()` resolves eagerly, creates a local signal; no hub registration. The `renderHtml` renders the frame. Good.

Potential issue: `PathlandSession` constructor with `hub != null` registers subscriptions during mount. The session isn't yet in `sessions` map, but the hub doesn't need that. The hub is passed in, so fine. If the session is closed before being put in the map (unlikely), `close` unregisters. Good.

Now, test coverage for initial value after a publish before subscription isn't there (we decided initial authoritative). Fine.

One more design concern: `PathlandSignalHub.publish` uses `List.copyOf(targets)`. If `targets` contains a subscriber that is being removed concurrently, the copy may include it; its `enqueue` checks `closed` and drops. Good.

One more: `SessionSubscriptions.enqueue` uses `pending.put` and `schedule`; if the session is closed between the check and `put`, close clears pending, then a value could be re-added after close. `drain` checks closed and clears. Fine. But `pending` could retain a value after close; `close` sets `closed` first, then clears; a racing enqueue could add after clear, then `schedule` may schedule a drain that sees closed and clears. Fine.

Now, a potential issue with `SessionSubscriptions.subscribe` being called during a render *after* the session is closed (e.g., a queued task runs after close)? `PathlandSession.submit` checks `closed` before running; the registry's `execute` may run a task that calls `emitter` after close? `close` is on the actor; tasks after close are dropped by `shuttingDown` only at registry shutdown, not per-session close. The `PathlandSession.submit` checks `closed`. But `dispatch`/`resync` methods don't check `closed`; the registry may dispatch after close? `close` removes the session from the map, so `session(...)` creates a new one; fine. `resync` after close via a stale reference? Not likely. Could add a `closed` check to public methods, but not necessary. `subscribe` throws if closed, which is good.

Now, full reactor compile. Run `mvn -q -DskipTests install` in `lib/java`. This builds all modules including demos. It may take a few minutes. Then optionally run the full reactor tests? The user asked to implement; we've run the relevant suites. Full install is enough for compile. Let's do it.

Now, think about whether the `PathlandSession.submit` method should be exposed on `SessionContext` (it is) and whether it can be called from a view during render. `SessionContext.current().submit { ... }` schedules; fine.

Potential issue: `SessionSubscriptions` implements `SessionContext.submit` by `actor.accept(task)`, where `actor` is `PathlandSession::submit`. That method schedules on the actor with context. Good. But `SessionSubscriptions.drain` is scheduled via `actor.accept(this::drain)`, which means the drain task is wrapped by `PathlandSession.submit` and will catch exceptions around `drain`. Good. `drain` itself catches per-signal exceptions. Fine.

Potential issue: `PathlandSession.submit` logs exceptions; `drain` applies and `signal.set` can throw; caught in `apply`. Good.

Potential issue: `SessionSubscriptions.close()` is called from `PathlandSession.close()` on the actor; it iterates `locals.keySet()`. If a drain is concurrently queued, it will see `closed` and clear pending. Good.

Now, one subtle issue: `PathlandRegistry.closeAllSessions` calls `session.close()` for all sessions, then `signalHub.clear()`. But `session.close()` calls `subscriptions.close()`, which calls `hub.unsubscribe`. Fine.

Another subtle issue: `PathlandRegistry.close(sessionId)` removes the session and calls `session.close()` on the actor. Good.

Now, the `PathlandSignalHub.subscribe/unsubscribe` methods are package-private. `SessionSubscriptions` is in the same package. Good. External code only uses `publish`, `subscriberCount`, `mount`.

Now, the `PathlandSignalHub.publish` `Objects.requireNonNull(topic, "topic")`; `subject` is required by `SubscriptionKey`. Good.

Now, check the Quarkus producer's `signalHub(PathlandHost host)` method name conflicts with the `PathlandHost.signalHub()` method? No.

Potential issue: In Quarkus, the producer method `signalHub` is in the same class as `host` producer; CDI may complain about a producer method with the same name as a field? No.

Now, docs correct.

Now, one more thing: `AGENTS.md` says "Current status: ... Complete" and we added. Good.

Now, maybe update `README.md`? Not necessary.

Now, consider the Rust workspace: no changes.

Now, check `git diff` for the status files to ensure no accidental weird replacements.

parts.text:
Now, final review of new files for any subtle issues.

`PathlandSignalHub`:
- `Set<SubscriptionSubscriber> targets = subscribers.get(key); int count = targets.size();` There's a race where the set can be emptied concurrently; `size()` is fine. `List.copyOf(targets)` may be empty; if count > 0 but the set is emptied before copy, the loop does nothing. Fine.
- `subscribe` uses `computeIfAbsent`; if a session unsubscribes concurrently? Sessions are actor-confined; only one actor per registry, and subscribe/unsubscribe run on the actor. External publish reads. Fine.
- `unsubscribe` uses `computeIfPresent`, removes and drops the set if empty. Good.
- `clear` at shutdown. Good.

`SessionSubscriptions`:
- `locals` is a `HashMap` accessed on the actor; `subscribe` may be called during SSR on the request thread and also from the session actor? For a given session, only one thread. Fine.
- `enqueue` from any thread.
- `drain` scheduled via `actor.accept`; if `actor` is `PathlandSession.submit`, it will schedule and set the context. If a session's `submit` is called from the actor thread, it schedules a new task. Fine.
- `scheduled` token: after `actor.accept(this::drain)`, if the actor is the registry's `execute` and the registry is shutting down, `execute` drops the task silently; `scheduled` stays true. The session is closing anyway. Fine.
- `close`: `locals.clear` while an actor drain might be running? `close` runs on the actor for live sessions, so no concurrent drain. For SSR, no hub. Fine.
- `subscribe` throws if closed. But `PathlandSession.close` sets `closed=true` and `subscriptions.close`; a queued render task won't run due to the `closed` check in `submit`. Fine.

`PathlandSession`:
- `closed` is volatile. `submit` checks it.
- `runWithContext` pushes the `SessionSubscriptions`, not the session. `SessionContext.submit` delegates to `PathlandSession.submit`, which pushes the context too. Fine.
- The constructor pushes the context before `app.newRoot()`. `subscriptions` is created. Good.
- The constructor's `applyEnvironment` calls `runWithContext` nested; fine.
- `close` calls `subscriptions.close` before `state.close`/`emitter.destroy`. Good. If an effect triggered by emitter.destroy? No.
- The `scheduler` field for SSR is `Runnable::run`; `submit` runs inline. SSR doesn't have a hub, so external updates aren't registered. `SessionContext.current().submit` from an SSR view would run inline on the request thread; fine.

`Topic`:
- `@JvmField val name` and equality. Good.
- The KDoc says "Two topics with the same name must therefore carry the same payload and subject types" — documented.

`Signals.topic`/`DeferredTopicSignal`:
- If a deferred signal is created and read in a session, it caches the resolved signal and context. If the context changes (a different session reuses the view instance), it re-resolves. Good.
- If the context is null, throws. Good.
- One subtlety: `Signals.topic` with a context returns the session signal directly; if the same view instance is reused across sessions, the eager signal from the first session would be reused in the second. But `topic()` is called during `body()` each render, not stored in the view (unless a field, which is a per-view-instance field). For a field initializer, the eager path only happens if the view is constructed inside a session; then the view is per-session in the normal model. If a singleton view is constructed outside, the deferred path handles context switching. Good enough.

Now, a potential issue: the `SessionContext` thread-local is set during `PathlandSession` constructor and `runWithContext`. But `Emitter.mount` calls `app.newRoot()`, and the `PathlandSession` constructor pushes the context. Good. However, `PathlandSession` is also constructed in tests directly (e.g., `PathlandSessionTest`) with no hub; context is pushed. Good. Any existing tests using `PathlandSession` with views that don't call `topic` are unaffected.

Now, the `PathlandRegistry.renderHtml` SSR session uses the 9-arg constructor, which delegates with `null` scheduler/hub. `renderHtml` itself doesn't push the context, but the constructor mounted and created subscriptions. The SSR render uses `sink.frame()`; no new `topic` calls. Good.

One more: `PathlandRegistry.session` creates the session inside an actor task. The `PathlandSession` constructor calls `applyEnvironment`, which sets `activePath`, triggering router effects; the context is set. Fine. Then the registry calls `session.connect`; no context needed.

Now, the full Java install passed, Quarkus/Spring suites passed, server-core/view-core suites passed.

Now, should we run `git diff --check` for whitespace. Do that. Also maybe `git status`.

Also clarify "broadcast" in distributed systems vs UI broadcast. A Redis channel publish is technically a broadcast to all node subscribers of that channel, but the channel can be scoped to topic+subject so only nodes with interest (or all nodes, filtered locally). Two patterns:
1. Global channel, every node receives every publish and filters to local subscribers. That's infrastructure broadcast with local targeted delivery. Simple but noisy.
2. Scoped channel per `(topic, subject)` or sharded channel, nodes subscribe only to keys they hold local subscribers for. More efficient but more complex (subscribe/unsubscribe churn).

"Cluster fan-out" would only be the *transport* step between servers:

```
publisher thread
      │  publish(topic, subject, value)
      ▼
  this node's hub ──► local subscribers for (topic, subject)
      │
      ▼  Redis / broker
  other node's hub ──► its local subscribers for (topic, subject)
      │
      ▼
  still only the matching sessions
```

So it is fan-out in the infrastructure sense (one publish reaches N servers), but it is **not a UI broadcast**. No node updates sessions that did not subscribe to that subject. A customer-43 session never sees customer-42's update, regardless of which node it lives on.

Two ways to implement it, if/when needed:

1. **Global channel, local filter** — every node receives every publish and forwards only to its matching local subscribers. Simplest; traffic scales with the number of nodes × publishes.
2. **Scoped/sharded channels** — channel key is derived from `(topic.name, subject)` (or a hash of it); a node subscribes only while it has at least one local subscriber for that key. More efficient, but requires subscribe/unsubscribe propagation and careful cleanup (e.g. when the last session for a subject closes).

Either way, the app-facing contract stays `publish(topic, subject, value)`; the current local `PathlandSignalHub` can be wrapped or replaced behind that interface without changing views. We need to think about how to model both scoped and unscoped topics in a strongly typed way. Options:

1. Two separate types:
   - `Topic<T>` (unscoped/global)
   - `ScopedTopic<T, S>` (subject-scoped)
   - Overloads: `topic(Topic<T>, initial)` and `topic(ScopedTopic<T,S>, subject, initial)`.
   - Publisher: `hub.publish(Topic<T>, value)` and `hub.publish(ScopedTopic<T,S>, subject, value)`.
   - Pros: compile-time guarantees; no nullable subject; no accidental mixing.
   - Cons: two concepts/some duplication; topic declarations specify which form; can't turn a scoped topic into a global one easily.

2. One generic type with an optional subject type:
   - `Topic<T, S>` where `S` can be `Unit` / `NoSubject` / `GlobalSubject`.
   - `topic(topic: Topic<T, Unit>, initial: T)` overload? Kotlin can overload on `Topic<T, Unit>` vs generic `topic<T,S>(Topic<T,S>, S, initial)`. Type erasure: `topic(Topic<T, ?>, ...)` signatures differ by parameter count (2 vs 3), so overload resolution is fine.  # Pathland Project - AI Agent Guide
 
 This document provides essential context for AI agents (or human contributors) working on the **Pathland** protocol. It captures the project's direction, architectural decisions, and implementation details to ensure consistency.

 ## Architecture: Rust Opcode Engine
 
 > The canonical core is a **Rust engine** that emits the application's
 > **declarative view structure** — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing, padding,
 > alignment — as a fixed **16-byte opcode ring buffer** into shared linear
 > memory, consumed by host renderers. View components and modifiers are written
 > in Rust with a SwiftUI-like API, and in Kotlin with the hand-written
 > **`dev.pathland.view.dsl` DSL** (reusable JVM library, Java 17+); both drive the
 > engine through the flat **native C ABI** (`pathland-view-native`) over a
 > zero-copy shared ring on desktop. Java hosts mount Kotlin views through
 > `PathlandApp`.
 
 ### The 16-byte Opcode Engine
 
 - Every opcode is exactly **16 bytes**: `Category (1B) | Command ID (1B) | Flags (2B) | A (4B) | B (4B) | C (4B)`, `#[repr(C, packed)]`, little-endian.
 - A 64-byte cache line holds exactly **4 opcodes** → L1-cache-friendly.
 - Opcodes live in a **ring buffer** in linear memory; the guest writes at `writeCursor`, the host reads from `readCursor`; frame boundaries via a monotonic `frameCount` in the header block.
 - **Both directions are binary**: a second **event ring** (host → guest) carries `EVENT`-category opcodes. The renderer writes raw inputs at `eventWriteCursor`; the guest drains them at `eventReadCursor`. Events are 16-byte opcodes through the engine, never a side-channel callback.
 - **Variable-length data** (strings, token paths) lives in a bump **arena**; opcodes reference entries by offset (`[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`), so every opcode stays 16 bytes. A second host-owned **event arena** mirrors this in the host → guest direction (shared-memory event strings, e.g. `TEXT_CHANGED`); over the network, host → guest strings ride the batch's string section.
 - **Window metadata** (`META::SET_WINDOW_METADATA`, field family `TITLE`/`DESCRIPTION`/`LOCALE`) carries the hosting surface's presentation metadata; renderers map it to their own chrome (browser `<title>`/meta description/`<html lang>`, GTK/Qt window title). It is root-scoped and signal-backed, so a route title is a computed over the router. Web-only artifacts (canonical/robots/sitemap) stay host-owned.
 - Spec: **`spec/OPCODE.md`** (primary) + **`spec/CONFORMANCE.md`** (golden vectors). Companion catalogs: **`spec/PRIMITIVES.md`** (views), **`spec/MODIFIERS.md`** (modifiers/properties), **`spec/EVENTS.md`** (events), **`spec/LAYOUT.md`** (frame & layout allocation contract) — draft IDs are allocated there spec-first.
 
 ### Declarative, not positioned (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The engine describes WHAT the UI is — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing,
 > padding, alignment — never WHERE it is. It does not compute layout and does
 > not emit rects.**
 
 - The engine emits **declarative structure** (`TREE` create/delete/insert/remove/move) + **constraint properties** (`PARAMETER` spacing/padding/alignment/FILL/HUG hints).
 - **Native elements everywhere**: each platform's renderer maps the opcode stream onto that platform's native elements — GTK4 widgets on desktop, DOM elements in the browser, HTML server-side — and those native elements lay themselves out. Never a generic canvas unless a platform has no native equivalent.
 - **Reactive emission**: emission is diff-based. Only the nodes that changed emit opcodes (property diffs via `SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_TEXT`, structural diffs via `TREE` opcodes). An unchanged tree emits **zero** opcodes. Signals in the application mark the tree dirty; the engine reconciles.
 - **Zero dynamic heap allocations** during steady-state emission (proven by test).
 
 ### no_std / wasm32 direction guard (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 `pathland-core` and `pathland-view` must remain `#![no_std]` + `alloc` and
 compile for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. This is the guarantee that the protocol
 core can still target a browser / embedded / remote projection later (goal #15,
 Quarkus SSR + WebSocket). The desktop path (`pathland-view-native`) is the only
 consumer today, but the core must not become desktop-only. Verify with
 `lib/rust/check-wasm.sh` (i.e. `cargo build -p pathland-core -p pathland-view
 --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`).
 
 ### Reactive signals (Angular-style)
 
 `pathland-core::signal` provides writable signals that live in the engine. A
 node binds its text (`Node::text_binding`), a property
 (`Node::property_bindings`) or a **string property** (`Node::string_bindings`,
 e.g. a media controller's `MEDIA_SOURCE`) to a `SignalId`; during emit the engine
 resolves the binding and records the dependency, and `Engine::set_signal`
 re-emits **only the bound nodes** (`SET_TEXT` / `SET_PROPERTY`) — no full tree
 walk. Signal values
 are one of `F32`/`U32`/`Bool`/`Enum`/`Str` (packed to the wire's `u32` value or
 arena string). Foreign hosts reach signals via the flat C ABI
 (`pathland_native_signal_create_*` / `signal_set_*` / `node_bind_text` /
 `node_bind_property`) and the Kotlin/JVM `Signal` type. Binding then calling `emit`
 records the dependency; a subsequent `set` is a partial emit. (Computed/derived
 signals + effects are the planned next step.)

 ### HTML base design (`design/`)
 
 The HTML renderer's built-in stylesheet is generated from a **three-layer Style
 Dictionary pipeline** plus hand-authored reset/component CSS (one built-in base
 design; no app-facing base-design selection):
 
 ```
 design/tokens/base/*.tokens.json      # internal palette + scales (not emitted)
 design/tokens/semantic/*.tokens.json  # protocol catalog semantics (emitted)
 design/tokens/component/*.tokens.json # per-component surface (emitted)
 design/html/{reset,components}.css    # hand-authored CSS consuming var(--pl-*)
 design/scripts/{build,dev,check}.mjs  # SD build, watcher/preview, validation
 design/build/base.css                 # generated: reset + tokens + components
 design/build/base.css.name            # content hash: base-<sha256-12>.css
 ```
 
 - Tokens are flat DTCG entries (`$value`/`$type`/`$extensions.pathland`) because
   the catalog has both leaf and group paths (`control.border` vs
   `control.border.width`). Dark values live on `$extensions.pathland.dark`;
   durations/z-index/`em` icon sizes are marked internal.
 - `npm --prefix design run build` generates
   `design/build/{tokens.css,manifest.json,base.css,base.css.name}`;
   `npm --prefix design run check` validates catalog coverage, layer direction,
   dark/forced-dark declarations, dimension/`isLengthToken` rules, and the CSS
   content hash.
 - `scripts/sync-design-css.sh` copies the bundle + name to
   `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/assets/` (committed; `--check` fails on
   drift). `css.rs` embeds both with `include_str!` (`builtin_css()` /
   `builtin_css_name()`); the Java port copies the same committed assets into
   its jar via Maven resources (`BaseCss`).
 - The renderer's library default is inline (`render_document`); the linked mode
   (`render_document_linked`, C ABI `pathland_html_render_linked` +
   `pathland_html_base_css[_name]`, Java `renderLinked`/`baseCss`/`baseCssName`)
   emits `{base}/base-<hash>.css`. The Spring Boot and Quarkus starters use it
   and serve the renderer-owned bytes immutable (global + mounted bases); token
   overrides/fit rules stay inline.
 - The Maven `refresh-ide` profile and CI run the design build + sync. Do not
   edit generated CSS by hand.
 
 ### Native C-ABI shim (`pathland-view-native` + `pathland-core-capi`)
 
 The **desktop/cross-language zero-copy path**: `pathland-view-native` exposes the
 flat world (the flat `builder`/`engine` surface) as `pathland_native_*` C
 functions with a **shared-memory ring** the host driver reads in place. Any
 language that links the dylib (Swift/Java via FFI) calls the flat surface —
 no per-component wrappers — and consumes opcodes zero-copy.
 
 `pathland-core-capi` (`libpathland_core`) is the **minimal ring C ABI** for the
 Kotlin DSL: `pathland_core_create`/`destroy`, `pathland_ring_buffer_push` (one
 raw 16-byte opcode), `pathland_core_arena_alloc`, frame boundaries, zero-copy
 `ring_ptr`/`ring_len`, and event drain/send. The Kotlin DSL
 (`dev.pathland.view.core.ffm`) binds it with **JNA** (lazily loaded, zero JNI) and
 owns the retained tree + diff emission itself.
 
 ### GTK4 Renderer (`pathland-render-gtk`)
 
 The desktop renderer: a single crate that owns **all** GTK/glib/pango usage and
 maps opcode frames **incrementally** onto native GTK widgets (a retained
 `id → gtk::Widget` map). Both the Rust demo and the Java demo render through
 it — the demos **never call GTK or Swing directly**:
 
 - Rust demo links `pathland-render-gtk` as an `rlib` and calls `GtkRenderer::run(...)`
   with a wake closure.
 - The Java/Kotlin desktop demo (`pathland-desktop-demo`) loads `pathland-render-gtk`
   as a `cdylib` via JNA and
   calls `pathland_gtk_run_ring(ring, on_event, width, height)` over the Kotlin view's
   `libpathland_core` ring; native inputs round-trip as `EVENT` opcodes through the shared
   ring. The renderer **writes** the events and **wakes** the host (no payload); the host
   drains the event ring itself via `pathland_core_drain_events`. Events are never
   delivered through a side-channel callback — they flow through the opcode engine.
   The demo mounts the Kotlin `MusicPlayerView` (the same shared view the web demos use) with the
   app-driven media contract: the renderer plays the tracks through a direct GStreamer
   `playbin` and reports `MEDIA_*` events back; the demo's web-style
   `/_pathland/assets/...` paths resolve against an extracted local asset root
   (`pathland_gtk_set_asset_root`).
 
 The renderer maps native inputs onto the raw `Event` surface via GTK4
 controllers (`Button::clicked` → pointer up, `EventControllerMotion` →
 pointer move/enter/leave), emitting events through the same `Pump::send_input`
 path.
 
 `pathland_gtk::run` passes an explicit empty argv to GTK (the process command
 line belongs to the embedding host — e.g. the JVM's `-cp`/`-D` flags — and must
 not be parsed as GTK options).
 
 ### Kotlin JVM authoring DSL (`dev.pathland.view.dsl`, in `lib/java/pathland-view-core`)
 
 The **sole JVM authoring surface**. It is the SwiftUI-like DSL shared by desktop,
 Spring Boot, Quarkus, and web apps. Components and modifiers:
 
 - `View` is an **open Kotlin interface** — the library ships `Text`/`Image`/`Color`/
   `Rectangle`, `VStack`/`HStack`/`ZStack`, `Spacer`, `Button`,
   `TextField(placeholder, WritableSignal<String>)`, `Video` (a
   `MediaController`'s surface), and application code defines its own views by
   extending `Component` or implementing `View`. **Media is a state object, not a
   view** (spec/MEDIA.md): `MediaController` owns the resource + transport as
   signals, a `Video` surface renders it, and **audio has no view** — the app
   binds its own buttons/sliders (`controller.attach()` materializes the
   controller's node once, outside any swapping branch).
 - **SwiftUI-style `body()` / reactive components**: composite views declare
   `View body()`; a signal read there subscribes that component, and a later write
   re-renders only that component and diffs its retained subtree. A signal bound
   to a node stays fine-grained and does not re-run the body. Plain
   `if`/`when`/`for` works; `ForEach` is the reactive list component.
 - **Builders and modifiers**: `VStack(spacing = 8f) { … }`, `Text("hi")`,
   `Button("Save") { … }`, `.padding`, `.frame`, `.fontSize`, `.background`,
   `.buttonStyle(BorderedButtonStyle)`, `.windowMetadata`, navigation intents, and
   the full modifier vocabulary. Styles are Kotlin values
   (`PlainButtonStyle`, `BorderedButtonStyle`, label styles, `NativeVideoStyle`).
 - **Builder scopes**: view blocks take a `PathlandScope` receiver. `PathlandScope`,
   `Navigation.Builder`, and modifier/style `Config` receivers share the
   `@PathlandDsl` marker, so an outer router/config receiver cannot be captured
   implicitly inside a nested view block (compile-time guard only; the
   thread-local `ViewScopes` stack still collects children).
 - **Persisted state**: `Component` provides `val count by state(0)` (auto-keyed
   by property name) or `state(0, "key")`, bound to the session's
   `PersistentState` before the first `body()` render — no annotation processor or
   kapt.
 - **Java hosting**: Java Spring Boot/Quarkus apps remain first-class hosts. A
   Java `PathlandApp` bean returns a Kotlin `View`
   (`return () -> MusicPlayerView.make();`); no Kotlin compiler or authoring DSL is
   needed in the host module. Every reusable Kotlin root exposes a public
   constructor or `@JvmStatic make(...)` factory with Java-friendly types.
 - **Consistency** with `pathland_core::constants` is enforced by the
   emitter/HTML tests (golden byte layout + round-trips).

 ## Project Vision
 
 **Pathland is a cross-platform, cross-language UI protocol** that enables retained-mode UI development with multiple renderer backends. It is **protocol-first**, meaning the protocol specification is the source of truth, not any particular implementation.
 
 **Primary Goal**: Write once, run anywhere - Enable UI code to be written once and deployed across web, mobile, desktop, and embedded platforms through different renderer implementations.
 
 **Status**: The Rust opcode engine (16-byte opcode, ring buffer, arena, diff-based reactive emission) is implemented and tested (`cargo test`). See the Architecture section above.
 
 ---
 
 ## CRITICAL ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES
 
 ### Principle 1: Renderer Statelessness (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The renderer MUST NOT retain application state.**
 
 - Renderers are **pure functions** of the opcode stream: same opcodes → same output
 - A renderer MAY retain its **rendered-output tree** (id → native element + computed layout) for drawing, hit-testing, and event routing — this is a cache of its own output, not state
 - The renderer MUST NOT retain component property values as business state, application control flow, or anything the application can change without emitting an opcode
 - The application owns the canonical retained UI tree
 - The engine emits **deltas only**; the renderer applies them to its native elements
 
 **Violation of this principle is a bug, not a feature.**
 
 ### Principle 2: Command-Based Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol transmits tree mutations as a stream of commands, NOT as serialized trees.**
 
 - Each frame is a **batch of delta commands** describing changes
 - Only **actual changes** are transmitted (diff-based reactive emission)
 - Protocol acts like a **VM instruction stream** / ABI
 - Deterministic, linear decoding without schema lookup or reflection
 
 ### Principle 3: Binary Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol MUST be binary.**
 
 - Open-source, cross-platform binary format
 - Fixed **16-byte instructions** in a ring buffer shared with the host via linear memory
 - Custom instruction-based bytecode, not schema-driven serialization
 - **Both directions are binary**: tree mutations (app → renderer) AND raw-input events (renderer → app) share the same instruction format, so the wire is language- and platform-agnostic

 ### Opcode Format
 
 Every opcode is exactly 16 bytes:
 
 ```
 [Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]
 ```
 
 See `spec/OPCODE.md` for the full format, ring buffer, arena, and frame lifecycle.
 
 ### Machine-readable protocol manifest
 
 `spec/protocol.tsv` is the target-neutral ID manifest emitted from
 `pathland_core::constants` by `pathland-protocol-manifest` (`cargo run -p
 pathland-protocol-manifest`). It contains only `kind`, `group`, `name`, and
 `value`; each language binding keeps its own representation and validates or
 reads the manifest. There is no Rust→JVM source generation.
 
 The JVM mirror is hand-written and checked by
 `pathland-view-core/src/test/java/.../ProtocolManifestTest`: every manifest row
 must match a Java constant, no extra public numeric constants may exist, and
 `ValueTypes.forProperty` must match `property_value_type`. CI regenerates the
 manifest from Rust and fails on drift.
 
 Engine behavior beyond individual opcodes is specified in `spec/ENGINE.md` and
 enforced by shared self-contained frame traces under `spec/engine-traces/`.
 `pathland-engine-golden` emits them from the Rust engine and the JVM
 `EngineTraceTest` compares its encoded frames byte-for-byte.
 
 ### Categories
 
 | Category | Value | Direction | Description |
 |----------|-------|-----------|-------------|
 | TREE | 0x01 | Guest → Host | Node create/delete/insert/remove/move |
 | PARAMETER | 0x02 | Guest → Host | Constraint properties (spacing, padding, …), design tokens |
 | EVENT | 0x03 | Host → Guest | Raw inputs: pointer down/move/up, key down/up |
 | META | 0x04 | Both | Reset, environment, window metadata |
 
 ### Component Types (u16)
 
 Grouped ranges (see `spec/PRIMITIVES.md`):
 
 | Group | Component | ID |
 |-------|-----------|----|
 | **Primitive Drawing (0x01–0x0F)** | TEXT | 0x01 |
 | | IMAGE | 0x02 |
 | | COLOR | 0x03 |
 | | SHAPE | 0x04 |
 | | DIVIDER | 0x05 |
 | | SPACER | 0x06 |

 ### Key Property IDs
 
 **Stack**: SPACING=0x0001, ALIGNMENT=0x0002, CONTENT_MARGINS=0x0005  
 **Text**: TEXT=0x000A, TEXT_ALIGNMENT=0x000C, LINE_LIMIT=0x000B, TRUNCATION_MODE=0x000D  
 **Style**: COLOR=0x100A, FONT_SIZE=0x1007, FONT_WEIGHT=0x1008, FONT_FAMILY=0x1009, BACKGROUND_COLOR=0x1001, BORDER_WIDTH=0x1003, BORDER_COLOR=0x1004, BORDER_RADIUS=0x1005, OPACITY=0x100D, VISIBLE=0x100E, Z_INDEX=0x100F, CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS=0x1010, PADDING=0x1011, PADDING_TOP/RIGHT/BOTTOM/LEFT=0x1012-0x1015  
 **Special**: WIDTH=0x100B (use -1=FILL, -2=HUG_CONTENT), HEIGHT=0x100C  
 **Semantic**: ROLE=0x2001, STATE=0x2002, ENABLED=0x2003, SELECTED=0x2004, EVENT_LISTENERS=0x2005 (u32 bitmask — which raw events a node wants reported), VALUE=0x2006, MIN_VALUE=0x2007, MAX_VALUE=0x2008, LABEL=0x200A, PROMPT=0x200B  
 **Binding/action**: ACTION_ID=0x2016, BINDING_ID=0x2017, TOGGLE_STYLE=0x2018 (Switch=0, Checkbox=1, Button=2)  
 **Media** (spec/MEDIA.md): MEDIA_CONTROLLER_ID=0x103A (a `VIDEO`'s controller), MEDIA_SOURCE=0x103B, MEDIA_MUTED=0x103C, MEDIA_LOOP=0x103D, MEDIA_RATE=0x103E; PLAYBACK_STATE=0x1035 / MEDIA_POSITION=0x1036 / MEDIA_VOLUME=0x1037 live on the controller
 
 ### Colors
 
 - Literal colors are **sRGB** with D65 white point, packed as `0xAARRGGBB`
 - A color property may instead carry a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference to a token path
 - Semantic token resolution and theme adaptation are **renderer-owned**
 
 ### Design Token System
 
 **Core Principle**: Application defines intent, overrides, and the theme.
 Renderer defines visual appearance, behavior, defaults, and interaction states.
 
 - The **application owns the theme**: token overrides (base = **light**, `dark.`-prefixed = **dark**) and token references in style properties. Token refs cover COLOR and non-color values (`Length` for spacing/padding/font size/radius/border/frame; `FontFamily.Token` for STRING) in the Rust and Kotlin DSLs.
 - The **renderer owns** default token values (light + dark, the full Tier-1 catalog), token resolution (including explicit `dark.` = forced dark and parent fallback), effective color-scheme detection, interaction states (hover, pressed, focus, disabled), and theme adaptation
 - `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` identifies tokens by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`) with the standard value-type encoding — there is no separate numeric tokenId system. A `dark.` prefix selects the dark variant (`dark.color.primary`); a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference whose path starts with `dark.` forces the dark value in either scheme
 - **Runtime theming**: `META::RESET_THEME` clears every app override; a replacement theme is reset + `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides in one frame. `META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME` forces `platform`/`light`/`dark`. Both are renderer state — no node is re-emitted. Java: `Emitter.replaceTheme`/`setColorScheme` + `PathlandSession.setTheme`/`setColorScheme`; Rust: `Engine::reset_theme`/`set_color_scheme`.
 - An unresolvable token reference leaves the property **unset** (renderer default), never an error or stale value.
 - The protocol MUST NEVER describe hover styles, click styles, visual transitions, conditional styling, or layout tuning for interaction states
 - **Deferred**: applying per-component tokens to native GTK/Qt leaf control chrome; web parent-path fallback.
 
 The HTML renderer's default token values are generated from `design/` (see
 "HTML base design" above). Full details: [Design Token System](./spec/OPCODE.md#design-token-system)
 and the canonical catalog / color-scheme contract in [spec/TOKENS.md](./spec/TOKENS.md).
 
 ---
 
 ## Implementation Guidelines
 
 ### Adding New Component
 1. Add to `component_type` in `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/src/constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Implement the component type in `pathland-core` (if it affects the retained tree)
 4. Implement native-element mapping in the target renderer (Goal 3–5)
 5. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Adding New Property
 1. Add to the appropriate property module in `constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Handle the value type in `pathland-core`'s diff emission (if a stack/text/size property)
 4. Implement in each renderer's property application
 5. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Modifying Protocol
 1. Update `spec/OPCODE.md` first (and `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` vectors)
 2. Update `constants.rs` and `pathland-core` encoding/emitters
 3. Run `cd lib/rust && cargo run -p pathland-protocol-manifest` and commit the
    updated `spec/protocol.tsv`
 4. Update the hand-written JVM protocol constants (the Java manifest test fails
    with the exact missing/stale row otherwise)
 5. If emission behavior changed, run
    `cargo run -p pathland-engine-golden -- --emit` and commit the trace fixtures
 6. Verify backward compatibility; update `pathland-core`/renderers + tests
 7. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Changing the Wire Format
 - Bump the wire `version` field in `spec/OPCODE.md` and `pathland-core`'s header (currently 1). Pre-release format changes are acceptable while version stays 1.
 
 ### Keeping implementation status updated (MANDATORY)
 
 **The agent MUST keep the per-project `status.md` files in sync with the code.**
 Whenever you land a protocol or renderer change — a new component/property/
 command/event, a new encoder/decoder, a new widget mapping, a new modifier or
 renderer feature, a test that proves new surface — **update the affected
 project's `status.md`** (Implemented / Not implemented / gaps) in the same
 change. The specs (`spec/`) describe the protocol contract only and MUST NOT
 carry implementation status; status lives in `status.md` next to each
 implementing project.
 
 ---
 
 ## Common Pitfalls
 
 ### NEVER Do These
 | Anti-Pattern | Why Wrong | Correct |
 |--------------|-----------|---------|
 | Renderer stores application state | Violates statelessness | Application owns the tree |
 | Engine computes layout / emits rects | Violates declarative model | Emit structure + constraints; native elements lay out |
 | Send full trees | Inefficient | Diff-based reactive emission |
 | String property names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | String component names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | Generic RGB | Ambiguous | Explicitly sRGB |
 | Hover styles in protocol | Renderer job | Define in theme |
 | Heap allocation in steady-state emission | Slow | Preallocated snapshot slab + arena |

 1. Read this file, `spec/OPCODE.md`, and `spec/ENGINE.md`

 ## Pathland Mindset
 
 **Always remember**:
 1. Protocol is King
 2. Renderers are Dumb (execute commands only)
 3. Applications are Smart (generate commands)
 4. Only Changes Matter (transmit mutations / reactive emission)
 5. Binary is Beautiful (efficient, deterministic)
 
 **When in doubt**: Check `spec/OPCODE.md`, the conformance vectors in `spec/CONFORMANCE.md`, and the companion catalogs (`spec/PRIMITIVES.md`, `spec/MODIFIERS.md`, `spec/EVENTS.md`, `spec/LAYOUT.md`), and the reference implementation (`pathland-core`). Ask: "Does this maintain stateless renderers?" "Does this only transmit actual changes?" "Does this describe WHAT the UI is, never WHERE?" "Is this representable as a 16-byte opcode in any language?"

 # External UI updates with topic subscriptions
 
 Pathland signals are single-threaded by contract: reads, writes, and effects run
 on the session's actor. Background work (Kafka/SmallRye `@Incoming` consumers,
 scheduled jobs, database notifications, other transports) runs on its own
 threads, so it must not set a view's signal directly.
 
 Topic subscriptions are the supported bridge. A view subscribes to a
 **strongly typed, always-scoped** topic and gets a normal `Signal<T>`; external
 code publishes a value for the same `(topic, subject)` pair from any thread, and
 only the sessions subscribed to that pair update. The runtime applies the value
 on each session's actor, so the existing effect/delta path is unchanged.
 
 ## 1. Declare the topic once
 
 A `Topic<T, S>` carries the payload type `T` and the subject type `S`. Topic
 identity is its name, so the view and the publisher share the same constant.
 
 ```kotlin
 object CustomerTopics {
     val NAME: Topic<String, Long> = Topic.of("customer.name")
     val ORDERS: Topic<List<Order>, Long> = Topic.of("customer.orders")
 }
 ```
 
 ```java
 public final class CustomerTopics {
     public static final Topic<String, Long> NAME = Topic.of("customer.name");
     public static final Topic<List<Order>, Long> ORDERS = Topic.of("customer.orders");
 
     private CustomerTopics() {}
 }
 ```
 
 ## 2. Subscribe in a view
 
 ```kotlin
 class CustomerOrdersView(
     private val customerId: Long,
     private val initialName: String,
     private val initialOrders: List<Order>,
 ) : Component() {
 
     private val name = topic(CustomerTopics.NAME, customerId, initialName)
     private val orders = topic(CustomerTopics.ORDERS, customerId, initialOrders)
 
     override fun body(): View = VStack(spacing = 8) {
         Text(name)                          // Signal<String>
         ForEach(orders) { OrderCard(it) }   // Signal<List<Order>>
     }
 }
 ```
 
 `topic(...)` returns a regular `Signal<T>`, so `Text(signal)`,
 `ForEach(signal)`, `signal.map { }`, and `computed { }` all work. Subscribing is
 idempotent per `(topic, subject)` within a session; repeated calls return the
 same local signal.
 
 Passing the wrong subject or payload type is a compile error: `NAME` requires a
 `Long` subject and a `String` value.
 
 ## 3. Publish from any thread
 
 The starter produces a `PathlandSignalHub` bean for the root mount (use
 `PathlandHost.signalHub(mount)` in a multi-app host). Publishing is
 non-blocking.
 
 ```java
 @ApplicationScoped
 public class CustomerConsumers {
 
     @Inject PathlandSignalHub hub;
 
     @Incoming("customer-name-changed")
     void onNameChanged(CustomerNameChanged event) {
         hub.publish(CustomerTopics.NAME, event.customerId(), event.name());
     }
 }
 ```
 
 Only sessions that subscribed to `(customer.name, event.customerId())` are
 updated. Two customers, two sessions: publishing customer 42's name never
 touches customer 43.
 
+## Global topics
+
+Some signals are app-wide rather than per-entity (a feature flag, a global
+counter, a service-status banner). Declare those with `Topic.global`:
+
+```kotlin
+object AppTopics {
+    val EVENTS: Topic<Long, GlobalSubject> = Topic.global("events.consumed")
+}
+```
+
+```kotlin
+// subscribe (every session that renders this line)
+val events = topic(AppTopics.EVENTS, 0L)
+Text(computed { "Events consumed: ${events.get()}" })
+```
+
+```java
+// publish (any thread)
+hub.publish(AppTopics.EVENTS, count);
+```
+
+A global topic is still subscription-targeted: only sessions that called
+`topic(AppTopics.EVENTS, …)` update. A session that never subscribed is
+untouched. There is deliberately no "publish to every subject" operation.
+
+The two-argument `topic(...)`/`publish(...)` overloads only accept
+`Topic<T, GlobalSubject>`, so a scoped topic cannot be published globally and a
+global topic cannot be published with a customer/order id. `GlobalSubject` is
+reserved as an application subject.
+
 ## Semantics
 
 - **Scoped, not broadcast.** The hub looks up subscribers by
-  `(topic.name, subject)`. There is no global publish path.
+  `(topic.name, subject)`. An unscoped global topic uses the singleton
+  `GlobalSubject` as its subject, so it reaches only the sessions that
+  subscribed to that topic — never every live session. There is no
+  publish-to-all-subjects path.
 - **Actor-confined.** Published values are applied on the session actor, so all
   signal reads/writes/effects keep the single-threaded contract.
 - **Latest wins.** Publishes are coalesced per session: at most one drain task is
   scheduled, and only the newest value per subscription is applied. A hot
   producer cannot flood the actor.
 - **`initial` seeds the signal.** A new session renders current data from its own
   source; subsequent changes arrive through `publish`. Late subscribers do not
   receive historical values.
 - **Session-scoped lifetime.** Subscriptions end when the session closes.
   `SessionContext.current()?.unsubscribe(topic, subject)` is available for dynamic
   subjects; SSR sessions subscribe for the first paint but do not register with
   the hub.
 - **Multi-app isolation.** Each mounted app has its own hub; `/` and `/billing`
   never see each other's topics.
 
 ## Notes
 
 - Declare a topic once and share the constant. The topic name is the wire
   identity (a future Redis fan-out can route on it); two topics with the same
   name must carry the same types.
 - The subject should be immutable with stable `equals`/`hashCode` — an id, a
   value class, or a record.
 - For an app-wide stream, use an explicit singleton subject
   (`object GlobalSubject`) as the `S` type; every subscription is still scoped.
 - If you need a lower-level escape hatch, `PathlandSession.submit(Runnable)` and
   `SessionContext.current()?.submit { }` run work on the session actor.

 package dev.pathland.view.core.subscription
 
 /**
  * A strongly typed, always-scoped subscription key.
  *
  * [T] is the published payload type and [S] is the subject (the thing the
  * subscription is about — a customer id, order id, tenant, conversation, …).
  * Both are checked at compile time by [subscribe] and
  * `PathlandSignalHub.publish`.
  *
  * Identity is by [name] (not by instance), so a topic declared once and shared
  * across modules — or across a process boundary — resolves to the same
  * subscription stream. Two topics with the same name must therefore carry the
  * same payload and subject types; declare each topic once in a shared constant
  * object.
  */
 class Topic<T, S>(@JvmField val name: String) {
 
     override fun equals(other: Any?): Boolean =
         this === other || (other is Topic<*, *> && other.name == name)
 
     override fun hashCode(): Int = name.hashCode()
 
     override fun toString(): String = "Topic($name)"
 
     companion object {
         /** A topic named [name] with payload type [T] and subject type [S]. */
         @JvmStatic
         fun <T, S> of(name: String): Topic<T, S> = Topic(name)
+
+        /**
+         * An unscoped (global) topic named [name]. Every session that subscribes
+         * with `topic(key, initial)` receives publishes; sessions that never
+         * subscribe are untouched.
+         */
+        @JvmStatic
+        fun <T> global(name: String): Topic<T, GlobalSubject> = Topic(name)
     }
 }
+
+/** Kotlin-friendly alias for an unscoped (global) topic. */
+typealias GlobalTopic<T> = Topic<T, GlobalSubject>

   that the Java DSL is gone); see #174.
 - **Java hosting**: a Java Spring Boot / Quarkus app mounts a Kotlin view through
   the Java-friendly `PathlandApp` functional interface
   (`return () -> MusicPlayerView.make();`). Kotlin roots expose public
   constructors and/or `@JvmStatic make(...)` factories.
 
 ## Package boundary
 
 - `pathland-view-core` is one Maven module: `core`/`engine`/`dsl` are logical
   subpackages inside it, with a few deliberate intra-module references
   (`Color`/`MediaController`/`Modified` materialize `PathlandNode`). Splitting
   them into separate artifacts would require a node SPI first.
 - Production runtimes/renderers (`pathland-server-core`,
   `pathland-render-html`) depend on this module. Framework starters remain
   DSL-neutral at compile time; they mount Kotlin-authored fixture views in test
   scope.

package dev.pathland.server

import dev.pathland.view.core.Environment

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList
import java.util.function.Consumer
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertFalse
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertThrows
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertTrue

/**
 * Topic subscriptions: strongly typed `(topic, subject)` routing, actor-confined
 * application, coalescing, and close/unsubscribe cleanup.
 */
class TopicsTest {

    private val name: Topic<String, Long> = Topic.of("test.customer.name")

    @Test
    fun publishTargetsOnlyTheSubscribedSubject() {
        val registry = registry(::probe)
        val customer42 = RecordingConnection()
        val customer43 = RecordingConnection()
        open(registry, "u42", "w42", "/42", customer42)
        open(registry, "u43", "w43", "/43", customer43)
        await { customer42.has("initial-42") && customer43.has("initial-43") }

        registry.signalHub().publish(name, 42L, "Alice")

        await { customer42.has("Alice") }
        Thread.sleep(100)
        assertFalse(customer43.has("Alice"), "customer 43 must not receive customer 42's update")
        assertTrue(customer43.has("initial-43"))
        assertEquals(1, registry.signalHub().subscriberCount(name, 42L))
        assertEquals(1, registry.signalHub().subscriberCount(name, 43L))
        registry.shutdown()
    }

    @Test
    fun everySessionForTheSameSubjectUpdates() {
        val registry = registry(::probe)
        val first = RecordingConnection()
        val second = RecordingConnection()
        open(registry, "a", "wa", "/42", first)
        open(registry, "b", "wb", "/42", second)
        await { first.has("initial-42") && second.has("initial-42") }

input.oldString:
Only sessions that subscribed to `(customer.name, event.customerId())` are
updated. Two customers, two sessions: publishing customer 42's name never
touches customer 43.
input.newString:
Only sessions that subscribed to `(customer.name, event.customerId())` are
updated. Two customers, two sessions: publishing customer 42's name never
touches customer 43.

## Global topics

Some signals are app-wide rather than per-entity (a feature flag, a global
counter, a service-status banner). Declare those with `Topic.global`:

```kotlin
object AppTopics {
    val EVENTS: Topic<Long, GlobalSubject> = Topic.global("events.consumed")
}
```

```kotlin
// subscribe (every session that renders this line)
val events = topic(AppTopics.EVENTS, 0L)
Text(computed { "Events consumed: ${events.get()}" })
```

```java
// publish (any thread)
hub.publish(AppTopics.EVENTS, count);
```

A global topic is still subscription-targeted: only sessions that called
`topic(AppTopics.EVENTS, …)` update. A session that never subscribed is
untouched. There is deliberately no "publish to every subject" operation.

The two-argument `topic(...)`/`publish(...)` overloads only accept
`Topic<T, GlobalSubject>`, so a scoped topic cannot be published globally and a

+## Global topics
+
+Some signals are app-wide rather than per-entity (a feature flag, a global
+counter, a service-status banner). Declare those with `Topic.global`:
+
+```kotlin
+object AppTopics {
+    val EVENTS: Topic<Long, GlobalSubject> = Topic.global("events.consumed")
+}
+```
+
+```kotlin
+// subscribe (every session that renders this line)
+val events = topic(AppTopics.EVENTS, 0L)
+Text(computed { "Events consumed: ${events.get()}" })
+```
+
+```java
+// publish (any thread)
+hub.publish(AppTopics.EVENTS, count);
+```

+`topic(AppTopics.EVENTS, …)` update. A session that never subscribed is
+untouched. There is deliberately no "publish to every subject" operation.

+The two-argument `topic(...)`/`publish(...)` overloads only accept
+`Topic<T, GlobalSubject>`, so a scoped topic cannot be published globally and a
+global topic cannot be published with a customer/order id. `GlobalSubject` is
+reserved as an application subject.

Implemented global topics on `feat/scoped-topics`.

## API

```kotlin
object CustomerTopics {
    val NAME: Topic<String, Long> = Topic("customer.name")                    // scoped
}

object AppTopics {
    val EVENTS: Topic<Long, GlobalSubject> = Topic.global("events.consumed") // global
}
```

```kotlin
val name   = topic(CustomerTopics.NAME, customerId, initialName) // scoped
val events = topic(AppTopics.EVENTS, 0L)                         // global

hub.publish(CustomerTopics.NAME, customerId, updatedName);
hub.publish(AppTopics.EVENTS, count);
```

- `GlobalSubject` is the reserved singleton (`"@global"`) used as the global scope.
- Two-argument `topic` / `publish` overloads only accept `Topic<T, GlobalSubject>`, so scoped topics can’t be published globally and global topics can’t be published with a customer id.
- Global means “every session subscribed to this topic”, not every live session; no publish-to-all-subjects path.
- Runtime unchanged: the hub still keys by `(name, subject)`, so coalescing, actor confinement, lifecycle, and cleanup are shared with scoped topics.
- Kotlin alias `GlobalTopic<T> = Topic<T, GlobalSubject>` added for readability.

- `TopicsTest`: 10 tests green — scoped targeting, multi-session, coalescing, actor thread, close/unsubscribe, field/deferred resolution, global reaches only subscribed sessions, and global/scoped same-name isolation.
- Quarkus + Spring `TopicSubscriptionsTest`: green — scoped customer 42 updates only 42, global `events` updates both sessions.
